Content: OODB 0098 E   TPFCS ERROR, ERROR CODE  errcode   errtext 
     

Where      errcode   The internal error code. 
 errtext   The text that describes the error. 
     

Last updated  
 Changed for  PUT11 . 
   

Explanation  
 ZOODB  command processing could not be completed because an error occurred. This error might or might not be internal. The error code from the associated environment block is displayed. 
   

System action  
 The command is rejected. 
   

User response  
 
 Take one of the following actions:   If this message was received in response to the  ZOODB MIGRATE  command for a data store, enter the  ZOODB DISPLAY  command for that data store to check whether the data store has an inventory. Migration is not supported for data stores that have an inventory.  z/TPF collection support  ( z/TPFCS ) does not use the inventory to manage the data store. If the data store has an inventory,  complete the following steps:   Enter the  ZOODB CHANGE  command for the data store with the  NOINVENTORY  parameter specified to remove the inventory. 
 Enter the  ZBROW QUALIFY  command for the data store. 
 Enter the  ZBROW NAME  command with the  DELETE  parameter specified to remove the DS_INVENTORY collection name from the data store. 
 Enter the  ZOODB MIGRATE  command again for the data store. 
   
 If this message was not received in response to a  ZOODB MIGRATE  command, or if the  ZOODB DISPLAY  command did not indicate that the data store was using an inventory when the migration failed,  complete the following steps:   Check for other errors that preceded this message to determine why  z/TPFCS  could not process the information for the specified request. 
 If you determine that the error is internal,  contact IBM® Support .

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB   
 
 With  z/TPF support for MongoDB , remote distributed platforms can access and update data in a  z/TPF  database by using the  MongoDB Query Language .   You do not need to change  z/TPF  application code to use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .   MongoDB  is a NoSQL database and treats data as documents.  MongoDB  documents are described by using   JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) , which is an open and human- and machine-readable standard to facilitate data exchange. The  z/TPF  database is not a NoSQL database, but you can create a  JSON  document from the data in the  z/TPF  database. 
       
 Access z/TPF data by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  The  z/TPF   Internet Daemon  ( InetD ) is used to access the  z/TPF  data by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  z/TPF support for MongoDB  is provided only for  z/TPFDF  databases.  
 
 MongoDB terminology  Some concepts in  z/TPFDF  and  MongoDB  are similar, but the terms to refer to these concepts might be different. 
 
 z/TPFDF database definition (DBDEF) considerations   z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports only R-type  z/TPFDF  files. Some settings in the  z/TPFDF  database definitions change the behavior of  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Add default keys by using z/TPFDF default key support  With  z/TPFDF default key support for z/TPF support for MongoDB , you can define default keys for  z/TPFDF  files in the  z/TPFDF collection descriptors  ( adbi.xml  files). 
 
 Setting up z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must define a  z/TPF  server for  MongoDB  before you can connect  MongoDB  remote clients to the  z/TPF system  by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .
z/TPF support for MongoDB
Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB security  To maintain a secure environment, you must implement controls to ensure that users have access only to data that they are authorized to access.  
 
 z/TPF user security   By using  z/TPF user security , you can define  z/TPF  user IDs, passwords, and privileges to  z/TPF  data and resources. You can use  z/TPF user security  only for   z/TPF support for MongoDB  applications.  
 
 Analyze the performance of z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can use   resource usage by owner name collection  on the  z/TPF system  to collect resource usage information for the  MongoDB  applications based on the owner name. You can specify the high-level qualifier and mid-level qualifier in the  resource usage by owner name configuration file  to collect resource usage information by specific categories.  
 
 Operations and coverage considerations for z/TPF support for MongoDB  There are operational considerations to remember when you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 User exits for MongoDB request processing  For each  MongoDB  request,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  provides two user exits, the pre-request user exit (UMON_pre_request) and post-request user exit (UMON_post_request) for you to control pre-request and post-request processing.  
 
 Filter collections by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  A filtered collection is a logical subset or view of a collection or a subset of logical records (LRECs) of a  z/TPFDF  file. As a database administrator, you can use filtered collections to control the visibility of the data in a collection.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB  programming   
 This information describes the  MongoDB  programming methodology that is used to interface with  z/TPF  data. 
 Examples that are provided in this information are one of the following types:   Programmatic examples that use the  MongoDB  Java™ client driver . 
 Shell based examples that describe the actual input document. You can use standard shell-based tools to send requests from a graphical user interface (GUI) or command line.  
           
 Connect to z/TPF support for MongoDB on the z/TPF system   
 
 Access the z/TPF database by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  When the  MongoDB  remote client connects to the  z/TPF system  and the  MongoDB  remote client is authenticated, the  MongoDB  remote client can access the  z/TPF  database.  
 
 Retrieve collections by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can retrieve individual collections from the  z/TPF  database after  MongoDB  remote clients access the database, for example, a  z/TPFDF  file that is named PNR.  
 
 Understand the ObjectId value in z/TPF support for MongoDB  In standard  MongoDB , documents that are saved in a collection require a unique ID field to be associated with the document. The ObjectId value is the representation of this unique identifier. In the  z/TPF system , the ObjectId value represents the file address of the prime block of the  z/TPFDF  subfile, which is unique for every subfile in a  z/TPFDF  file. The ObjectId value, in the  z/TPF system , is a 12-byte value that consists of an 8-byte hexadecimal file address that is right justified. 
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB data definition considerations  When you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , the  DFDL schema file  describes the contents of the  z/TPFDF  file. The  DFDL schema file  for the  z/TPFDF  file defines the field names and data types for the  z/TPFDF  binary data.
z/TPF support for MongoDB programming
Use automatic indexing rules for z/TPF support for MongoDB  With standard  MongoDB  servers, you can add indexes for fields in the document that allows optimized retrieval when the document is located by using that field. The indexes for these fields are maintained by the standard  MongoDB  server. Maintenance of these indexes is transparent to the end user who accesses the standard  MongoDB  server. 
 
 Retrieve documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can retrieve the documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you get a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Insert documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can insert documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Update documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can update documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Remove documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can remove documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Logging for z/TPF support for MongoDB  With logging for  z/TPF support for MongoDB , you can log  MongoDB  requests and responses and send the logging data to a server in binary JSON (BSON) format.  
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB error messages  When you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , certain situations might   cause the  z/TPF   MongoDB  server to return  an error. For example,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  returns an error to the  MongoDB  client when a user tries to update a document but does not have authority to update.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB  ( APARs  PJ42292 and PI33010)   
 z/TPF support for MongoDB   provides the ability to access  z/TPFDF  databases from remote distributed systems by using the standard  MongoDB  query language without requiring changes to z/TPF applications.  
 Previously, to request access to the  z/TPF  data on the  z/TPF system  from a remote distributed system, custom applications were required on the  z/TPF system  and the remote distributed systems that access the  z/TPF  data. The custom  z/TPF  applications required accessing the  z/TPF  databases and formatting  z/TPF  binary data for the remote distributed system applications. Implementing the custom applications on the  z/TPF system  might have the following results:   The implementation of the custom interfaces was time consuming.  
 
 z/TPF  application programmers and remote application developers were involved to maintain custom interfaces.  
 Different custom interfaces might need to be developed and deployed, because remote distributed systems might require different formats and functionality.  
     With  z/TPF support for MongoDB , remote distributed systems can access the  z/TPFDF  databases by using the standard  MongoDB  clients. Standard  MongoDB  clients exist in different programming languages, and you can install standard  MongoDB  clients on different remote distributed platforms.  
 z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports many  MongoDB  programming services. With these  MongoDB  programming services, you can get information or access documents in the  z/TPFDF  databases.  
 Accessing  z/TPFDF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB  does not require any changes to the  z/TPF  applications. However, to use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , the code must be built with the  GCC  4.6 ( version tpf-11r1-13 or later ) or the Dignus Systems/C or Systems/C++ V1.98 (version 1.98.68 or later) compiler.  
 For more information about  APARs   PJ42292  and PI33010, see the APEDITs.

Content: TO2_atRBAPut: Store data in a BLOB         This function is used to either add data to a binary large object (BLOB), completely replace the contents of a current BLOB, or change a specific set of bytes in a BLOB. If the BLOB is larger than a single transmission buffer, multiple  TO2_atPut  functions can be entered as each buffer is received to add the new data to the BLOB. The number of bytes stored will be the length specified or the size of the BLOB, whichever is smaller. To completely replace the data in an existing BLOB, call the  TO2_makeEmpty  function before the first  TO2_atRBAPut  is entered with the replacement data.

TO2_ATPUT_ONLY   This is the only  TO2_atRBAPut  function call.  The BLOB is completed and can be closed out.

Content: Configuring your  z/TPF system  for  z/TPFDF remote subfile support 
   
 Before you can use  z/TPFDF remote subfile support ,  you must configure   z/TPFDF remote subfile support  on your  z/TPF system . 
 

Before you begin    Ensure that you  configured the  z/TPF system  for  z/TPF support for Java™ . 
   

Procedure  
 
 
 Complete the following steps to build and load all components for the tpfrdsClient  z/TPF application manager for Java (JAM) . The tpfrdsClient  JAM  is not built or loaded by default.      Set the  TPF_SBTPFRDS  function switch for the   z/TPF system  environment to  YES . To set function switches for your environment, follow the instructions in the  tpftools/include_ztpf/tpf.function_switch_overrides  file. 
 
 Build all programs in the  base/cntl/tpfrds.cntl  control file by entering the following command:      bldtpf base/cntl/tpfrds.cntl   
 
 Load all files that are listed in the  base/cntl/tpfrds.loadfile  load file to your  z/TPF system . 
   
 
 Ensure that the local  IBM® MQ  queue manager is defined on your  z/TPF system  by completing the following steps:     Enter  ZMQSC DISPLAY QMGR  to display the local  IBM MQ  queue manager on your  z/TPF system . 
 If the local  IBM MQ  queue manager does not exist, enter the  ZMQSC DEFINE QMGR  command to define the queue manager. 
   
 
 Define a  IBM MQ  process on your  z/TPF system  for use by all remote data store update queues by entering the following command:      ZMQSC DEFINE PROCESS-TPFRDS.UPDATEQ.PROCESS APPLICID-DRDQ   
 
 
 Deploy the  OpenAPI descriptor  for the common deployment REST service by entering the following command:     ZMDES DEPLOY FILE-tpffdes.swagger.json
#

Content: z/TPF C/C++ APIs
TPFxd_sync: Verify queued information   
 
 TPFxd_write: Write to an external device   
 
 TPFxd_writeBlock: Write core block images to the external device   
 
 tppc_activate_on_confirmation: Activate a program after confirmation received  This function is an extension to the LU 6.2 architecture. This function allows the issuing  z/TPF  ECB to exit after sending out a  tppc_confirm ,  tppc_deallocate  with  DEALLOCATE_TYPE_CONFIRM  or  tppc_prepare_to_receive  with  PREP_TO_RECEIVE_TYPE_CONFIRM  request.  TPF/APPC  then activates a different ECB at the program specified when the reply to the confirm request has arrived and has been processed. 
 
 tppc_activate_on_receipt: Activate a program after information received  This function is an extension to the LU 6.2 architecture. This function allows the issuing  z/TPF  ECB to exit and activate a different ECB at the program specified after information has been received. The information received may be data, conversation status, or a confirmation request. 
 
 tppc_allocate: Allocate a conversation  This function allocates a conversation between a  z/TPF  transaction program and a transaction program in a remote LU. 
 
 tppc_confirm: Send a confirmation request  This function sends a confirmation request to the remote transaction program and waits for the confirmation reply.  This allows the 2 programs to synchronize their processing. 
 
 tppc_confirmed: Send a confirmation reply  This function sends a confirmation reply to the remote transaction program. This allows the 2 programs to synchronize their processing. The local  z/TPF  transaction program can call this function when it receives a confirmation request from the remote transaction program. 
 
 tppc_deallocate: Deallocate a conversation  This function deallocates the specified conversation from the transaction program. An implied FLUSH is executed, and the resource ID becomes unassigned when the deallocation is complete.
z/TPF C/C++ APIs
tppc_flush: Flush data from local LU buffer  This function allows the application to transmit any data from the data buffer of the local LU, including an ATTACH from the  tppc_allocate  function. 
 
 tppc_get_attributes: Get information about a conversation  This function returns information pertaining to a conversation. 
 
 tppc_get_type: Get conversation type  This function returns the conversation type, which can be either basic or mapped. 
 
 tppc_post_on_receipt: Set posting active for a conversation  This function causes the conversation to be posted when information is available for the transaction program to receive. The information can be data or conversation information. The  tppc_wait  function should be called after this function in order to wait for posting to occur.  Alternatively,  tppc_test  can be called after this function in order to determine when posting has occurred. 
 
 tppc_prepare_to_receive: Change to receive state  This function changes the conversation from  send  to  receive  state in preparation to receive data. The change to  receive  state is completed as part of this function. The execution of this function includes the function of the FLUSH or CONFIRM verb. 
 
 tppc_receive: Receive information  This function waits for information to arrive on the specified conversation and then receives the information. If information is already available, the information is received without waiting. The information received may be data, conversation status, or a confirmation request. 
 
 tppc_request_to_send: Request change to send state  This function notifies the remote transaction program that the local  z/TPF  transaction program is requesting to enter  send  state for the conversation. The conversation changes to  send  state when the local  z/TPF  program subsequently receives a SEND indication from the remote program.
#

Content: z/TPF  C/C++ APIs       The following contains an alphabetic listing of the  z/TPF  general services, which consists of C/C++ functions and macros. C/C++ APIs are used by  z/TPF  applications that need system services. No special authorization is required by the C/C++ APIs, although some parameters may be restricted, as noted. 
 The following information is shown for each  z/TPF  C/C++ API: 
 Purpose:  Describes how and why you use the API. 
 Last updated:  Provides historical information about when the API was added, changed, obsoleted, or replaced. 
 Format:  The API prototype and a description of any parameters. 
 Normal return:  Lists what is returned when the requested service has been performed. 
 Error Return:  Lists what is returned when the requested service could not be performed. Specifying incorrect API parameters results in a system error and exits. 
 Programming Considerations:  Lists any additional considerations for using the API, including any restrictions or limitations. 
 Example:  Provides one or more examples that show you how to code the API. 
 
 Note:  The  TPF/APPC  basic conversion functions and mapped conversion functions document return codes instead of the normal and error returns that are documented for all other  z/TPF  APIs.           
 abort: Terminate program abnormally   
 
 accept: Accept a connection request   
 
 activate_on_accept: Activate a program when the client connects   
 
 activate_on_receipt: Activate a program after data received  The  activate_on_receipt  socket function allows the issuing ECB to exit and activate a different ECB at the program specified after information has been received.
z/TPF C/C++ APIs
activate_on_receipt_of_TCP_message: Activate a program after a TCP message is received  The  activate_on_receipt_of_TCP_message  function allows the issuing ECB to exit and activates a specified program in a new ECB when a message arrives on a TCP socket. The message adheres to a specific format and contains a header that includes the length of the message. The length of the message is the length of the header and message text. The maximum message size, including the header, is 1048576 bytes. The entire message is passed to the application program. 
 
 activate_on_receipt_of_TCP_message2: Activate a program after a TCP message is received  The  activate_on_receipt_of_TCP_message2  function allows the issuing ECB to exit and activates a specified program in a new ECB when a message arrives on a TCP socket. The message adheres to a specific format and contains a header that includes the length of the message. The length of the message is the length of the message text, and does not include the length of the header. The maximum message size, including the header, is 1048576 bytes. The entire message is passed to the application program. 
 
 activate_on_receipt_with_length: Activate a program after data of specified length received  The  activate_on_receipt_with_length  socket function allows the issuing  entry control block  ( ECB ) to exit and activate a different  ECB  at the program specified after information with a specified length has been received. 
 
 addlc: Add a block to the z/TPF task dispatch list  This function adds a block to a specified  z/TPF system  task dispatch list (CPU loop list). 
 
 alarm: Schedule an alarm   
 
 atexit: Call a function at normal program termination   
 
 attac: Attach a detached working storage block   
 
 attac_ext: Attach a detached working storage block

Using programmed symbols for IBM 3270   
  Programmed Symbols (PS) , an optional feature on the IBM® 3270 terminal, lets you store and access up to six character sets of 190 characters each that are user-definable and program-loadable. 
 After the coded graphic character sets have been loaded into the PS buffers, they can be used on a field-by-field basis by using Message Format Service (MFS). 
 If the PS buffers are desired and have not been loaded, they must be loaded by a VTAM® application or by some other means. 
         
 Determining whether the buffers are loaded  If you know that the buffers have already been loaded with the desired programmed symbols, you do not need to resend the entire load programmed symbols data stream.  
 
 Loading the PS buffer  If the operator knows the PS buffers need to be loaded (because the device was just powered on), enter a response-mode transaction that loads programmed symbols by using an installation-written application program that loads PS buffers. 
 
 Solving load problems  If a hardware error occurs while loading a programmed symbols buffer, IMS performs series of predefined actions. 
 
 Reloading the PS buffer  When a message is waiting on the IMS queue for a terminal and requires programmed symbols that are not loaded, you must load the programmed symbols. 
 
 Application design considerations  A message that uses programmed symbols is different from other IMS output messages; it relies on the correct programmed symbol (PS) buffer content for its presentation.

Answer: IMSを再起動するには、以下の手順に従ってください。  
1. **IMS ジョブ・ストップ（STOP）コマンドを実行**  
   まず、現在実行中の IMS インスタンスを停止します。このコマンドは CICS または TSO 環境から実行できます。  
   ```jcl
   //STOPIM  EXEC PGM=IEFBR14,COND=EQ,PARM='STOP(IMS)'
   //SYSIN   DD  DUMMY
   ```  
   あるいは、IMS の操作マニュアルに記載されている「STOP IMS」コマンドを使用してください。  

2. **IMS ジョブ・スタート（START）コマンドを実行**  
   IMS を停止した後、再起動します。START コマンドを使用して IMS を起動します。  
   ```jcl
   //STARTIM EXEC PGM=IEFBR14,COND=EQ,PARM='START(IMS)'
   //SYSIN    DD  DUMMY
   ```  
   または、IMS の操作マニュアルに記載されている「START IMS」コマンドを使用してください。  

3. **必要に応じて、IMS リソース・データベース（RECON）の更新**  
   IMS を再起動する前に、必要に応じて RECON データベースを更新しておくことがあります。特に、新しいユーザーアユイキットやパラメーターの変更がある場合には、`REFRESH USEREXIT` コマンドを使用してください。  
   ```jcl
   //REFRESH EXEC PGM=DFSMSVRC,PARM='REFRESH(USEREXIT)'
   //SYSIN    DD  DUMMY
   ```  

4. **監視と確認**  
   IMS が正常に再起動したかどうかを確認するために、IMS のログや CICS トレースを確認します。エラーメッセージがないことを確認してください。  

これらの手順に従うことで、IMS を安全に再起動できます。詳細な手順やエラー処理については、IBM の IMS 操作マニュアルや CICS 操作マニュアルを参照してください。

Content: Examples of grammar definitions       
 Grammar: cc++   Accepts any character string between 2 and 4 letters. If the IPRSE_NOMIXED_CASE option is used the input string must contain all uppercase letters.   Possible input strings: ABCD or ABC or AB and so on. 
   
 
 Grammar:    ccd+   Accepts 2 letters followed by 1 or 2 decimal digits. If the IPRSE_NOMIXED_CASE option is used both letters must be uppercase.   Possible input strings: XY23 or XY2 and so on. 
   
 
 Grammar:    cc*   Accepts any character string with at least 2 letters. If the IPRSE_NOMIXED_CASE option is used the input string must contain all uppercase letters.   Possible Input Strings: AB, or ABCD, or ABCDEFGHILLLO 
   
 
 Grammar:    cc.dd   Accepts the following input strings:     Two letters followed by 2 decimal digits:               AA.12
            XY.66 
 
 A period followed by 2 decimal digits:                 .45 
 
 Two letters followed by a period:               AB.  If the IPRSE_NOMIXED_CASE option is used the input string must contain all uppercase letters. 
     
 
 Grammar:    (cc)*   Accepts 2 letters or any number of multiples of 2 letters with periods between each 2 letters.   Input string: XX.XX.AB.CD or LA or DO.RE.MI and so on.  If the IPRSE_NOMIXED_CASE option is used the input string must contain all uppercase letters.   
 Example   Grammar    www  Accepts 3 characters, including letters, decimal digits, underscores (_), and asterisks (*). If the IPRSE_NOMIXED_CASE option is used all of the letters must be in uppercase. An asterisk can match one or more w characters.   Input Strings:
*X or ABC or *1B
* or ** or ***
A* or *B* or 1*2 or 0** and so on. 
 
   See  Examples  for a complete example that shows the grammar, the parsing, and the call to a function to process the parsed output.

Content: EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
Specifying an EBCDIC file encoding to use with the language servers    
 The language servers parse programs using the IBM-037 code page by default. If your program uses a different target encoding on z/OS, you must specify an EBCDIC code page for the language server to use, so it can compute the correct line length. This encoding should match the EBCDIC encoding used, when the file is placed back on z/OS. This functionality currently supports only the COBOL and PL/I language servers. 
 Here is how Z Open Editor evaluates what encoding to pass to the language server: 
 
 
 For local COBOL or PL/I programs, you must configure the  zopeneditor.encodings.filePatterns  settings object. 
 
 
 This setting maps file name glob patterns to an EBCDIC file encoding. These patterns is specified as glob patterns. A single asterisk  *  matches any number of characters within a path segment, including none. A double asterisk  **  matches any number of path segments, including none. For example,  { **/COBOL/*.cbl : IBM-930 }  assigns any file paths that contains a directory named  COBOL  ending with a  .cbl  extension an encoding of  IBM-930 . ([Learn more about how to specify glob patterns.](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns)) 
 
   
 
 For remote programs (accessed through Zowe Explorer), you can do any of the following: 
 
 
 If an RSE API profile is used to access the file (such as a data set opened in Zowe Explorer), Z Open Editor first looks for an encoding specified by your RSE mappings as documented  above  (either in a  rseapi  profile in your  zapp.yaml  or the location in the  zopeneditor.zowe.defaultRseConversionMappingsFile  setting). 
 
 
 If no RSE mappings exist or if you are using a z/OSMF profile to access the file, you can specify an encoding in the Zowe Explorer profile you are using to access the program (see the  encoding  property example in this  section ).
EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
You can use the  zopeneditor.encodings.filePatterns  user setting for remote files, but you must adjust the glob pattern to match to remote files in the Zowe Explorer filesystem (described  here ). 
 
   
   These settings only control what encodings are passed to the language servers. To control encodings used for file conversions when you upload or download z/OS resources, use an RSE API mappings file or  rseapi  ZAPP profile, or specify the  encoding  property in your Zowe profile. 
 When a program is opened that is associated with an encoding using one of the methods above, a counter titled "EBCDIC Byte Count" is visible in the Visual Studio Code status bar. This counter displays two numbers: the number of bytes in the line up of the cursor's current position (accounting for the source code page), and the maximum number of bytes enabled in the line (controlled by the  zopeneditor.language.maximumLineLength  setting). As with the previous functionality, this counter only displays for COBOL and PL/I programs. 
 If the language server detects double-byte characters, it displays guillemets (»«) at the position of the SOSI codes, when applicable. These guillemets are decorative and not stored with the program or affect its line length.
EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
Character conversion using .gitattributes    
 The  .gitattributes  file enables you to specify how files are encoded when it is checked out to the directory you work and when it is stored in the Git repository. This is particularly useful to handle double-byte characters. 
   How it works   
 
 
 User Build from VS Code: When you perform a user build on an existing COBOL file that contains double-byte characters, the  .gitattributes  settings ensure that the file is encoded in IBM-930 when it is checked out to the working directory. 
 
 
 Build process: During the build process, the file is uploaded to the specified USS folder with the correct encoding that is mentioned in the  .gitattributes . 
 
 
 File display in VS Code: When you open the file in VS Code, the double-byte characters are correctly converted from IBM-930 to UTF-8. 
 
     Example workflow   
 
 
 Update the  .gitattributes  file located at the root of the repository with the following line. This specifies an encoding of IBM-930 for all files in the repository with the  .cbl  file extension:  *.cbl zos-working-tree-encoding=ibm-930 git-encoding=utf-8 . 
 
 
 Perform a user build from VS Code on an existing COBOL file that contains double-byte characters using the right-click menu. 
 
 
 During the build process, the  zos-working-tree-encoding  parameter specifies the code page used to encode files that are uploaded to USS or MVS. 
 
 
 Wait for the build process to complete. Once finished, the COBOL file is uploaded to the specified USS folder using the encoding from  .gitattributes . 
 
 
 When opened in VS Code, the Japanese characters is correctly converted from IBM-930 to UTF-8. 
 
     Example file with double-byte characters   こんにちは、世界！ //* Hello world!
これはテストファイルです。 //* This is a test file.
IBM-930エンコーディングを使用しています。 //* Using IBM-930 encoding.

Answer: CA証明書や自己署名証明書は、使用する際にどこにインストールすべきですか？  
これらの証明書は、一般的に以下の場所にインストールする必要があります。  

1. **CICS 環境**: CICS トランザクションサーバーの設定ファイル（例えば、RSE 経由でアクセスする場合）に証明書を指定し、RSE API プロファイルや Zowe Explorer プロファイルでのエンコーディング設定を行います。  
2. **IMS 環境**: IMS 用の JCL またはプロシージャー内で、証明書を使用するための PARMLIB や PROCLIB に設定し、必要に応じて RSE マッピングファイルを使用してエンコーディングを指定します。  
3. **DB2 環境**: DB2 の接続設定（例えば、JDBC ドライバーや DRDA 接続）で、証明書を含むキーストア（例えば、PKCS#12 ファイル）を指定し、DB2 のプロパティファイルや環境変数で証明書のパスを設定します。  
4. **MQ 環境**: IBM MQ のキャンバス（例えば、MQSC スクリプトや管理ツール）で、証明書を使用するためのキーストアやトラストストアを指定し、MQ の構成ファイル（例えば、qm.ini や amqcllrb.a）で証明書のロケーションを設定します。  
5. **TSO/ISPF 環境**: TSO/ISPF のセッションで、証明書を使用するための RACF データベースやプロファイルに証明書を格納し、ISPF の設定オプションで証明書のパスを指定します。  
6. **USS 環境**: Unix サーバー上で、証明書を含むキーストアを適切なディレクトリ（例えば、/etc/pki/tls/certs など）に配置し、アプリケーションの設定ファイルで証明書のパスを指定します。  

これらの設定により、各システムが証明書を正しく認識し、安全に通信できるようになります。

[Rank 2] Title: IBM zSecure Syntax rules
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/szs/3.2.0?topic=syntax-rules
Score: 0.1661752164363861
Content: Syntax rules     Follow these rules when you code  CARLa  commands: 
   CARLa commands generally consist of a command keyword and parameters. 1 
 
 Separate parameters with blanks or commas; multiple blanks and commas are allowed. 
 Start a string literal with a quotation mark (single, double, or left quotation mark). 
 End a string literal with a matching quotation mark. (A string can contain other quotation marks or comment markers.) 
 Start a comment with /* (forward slash followed by an asterisk). 
 End a comment with */ (reverse the characters used to start the comment). A comment can contain quotation marks. The /* begin-comment marker has no special meaning within the comment. 
 String literals and comments can cross a line boundary. 2  No other parameters can cross a line boundary. 
 A sequence of DBCS (Double-byte Character Set) characters in a line is initiated by a shift-out character and terminated by a shift-in character in the same line.
Syntax rules
A sequence of DBCS (Double-byte Character Set) characters in a line is initiated by a shift-out character and terminated by a shift-in character in the same line. 
 Within a string literal crossing a line boundary, if a continuation line starts with a shift-out (SO) character, optionally preceded by SBCS (Single-byte Character Set) space characters, lines immediately preceding this line are trimmed away if they entirely consist of SBCS spaces. Trailing SBCS spaces in the line before these blank lines, if any, are trimmed away as well. If the trimmed line ends with a shift-in (SI) character and the continuation line starts with an SO character, these SI and SO characters are trimmed away, too.  For instance, if a string literal line ends with 監, an SI character, and an SBCS space, and if the next line starts with an SO character and 査, the CARLa parser interprets this as 監査, without any characters between 監 and 査.  If SBCS spaces before a DBCS string are significant, for example, for alignment purposes, these spaces can sometimes be placed before the SO character initiating the DBCS string, in the same line as the SO. Alternatively, pairs of SBCS spaces can be represented as DBCS space characters right after the SO. If the number of significant SBCS spaces is odd, a single SBCS space can be placed right before the SO, in the same line as the SO. If the SO is found at the beginning of a line, and if it is inconvenient to insert space characters around it in the same line, it is possible to add a prefix to a new line containing significant SBCS spaces, an SO character, an SI character, and trailing SBCS spaces. 
 Commands can cross a line boundary; this generally requires a comma at the end of the line to indicate that more parameters will follow.
#

Content: TO2_add: Add an element to a collection         This function adds the specified data to the collection at the position appropriate for the type of collection being added:     Array   Appends the element to the current end of the collection. 
 Bag   Adds the element to the collection. 
 BLOB   Appends the data to the current end of the collection. 
 Key Bag   Not supported. 
 Key Set   Not supported. 
 Key Sorted Bag   Not supported. 
 Key Sorted Set   Not supported. 
 Keyed Log   Appends the element to the logical end of the collection and updates the secondary index with the key field value. The secondary index is a user-defined key field that can be used for searching. 
 Log   Appends the element to the logical end of the collection. 
 Sequence   Appends the element to the current end of the collection. 
 Set   Adds the element to the collection after checking to make sure the element is not a duplicate. 
 Sorted Bag   Adds the element to the collection in the correct sequence position. Elements with the same sort field values are added in a first-in-first-out (FIFO) order in the collection. 
 Sorted Set   Adds the element in sort sequence determined by the sort field.

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=glossary-z-entries
Score: 0.46072515845298767
Content: Z – glossary entries       Z-messages   Commands. Also referred to as  Z-messages  because the first character of the message is always Z or  functional messages . 
 zero suppression   The substitution of blanks for leading zeros in a number.  For example, 00057 becomes 57 when using zero suppression. 
 
 z/TPF  API functions   C library functions that provide  z/TPF -specific services. 
 z/TPF application requester   In the  z/TPF system , support that allows  z/TPF  application programs to read and write directly to any database server that is compliant with Distributed Relational Architecture (DRDA), such as  Db2® . 
 
 z/TPF  block   One of the storage blocks that can be attached to the CBRW of an ECB. The  z/TPF system  has 128-, 381-, 1055-, and 4095-byte blocks. 
 
 z/TPF collection support file system  ( TFS )   A processor-shared, subsystem-unique file system that uses  z/TPF collection support  as its storage mechanism. 
 
 z/TPF -compatible compiler   A compiler that is Linux® but produces code in the  executable and linking format (ELF)  that runs correctly on the  z/TPF system . All  z/TPF -compatible compilers are  ELF -compatible. 
 
 z/TPF  complex name   See  complex name . 
 z/TPF file system support   A data storage facility that includes multiple file systems that emulate POSIX-compliant hierarchical file systems using the  z/TPF  database. See also  fixed file system (FFS) ,  memory file system (MFS) ,  pool file system (PFS) , and  z/TPF collection support file system (TFS) . 
 z/TPFAR   
 z/TPF application requester . 
 z/TPFCS   
 z/TPF collection support . 
 z/TPFCS database   A database that provides a set of services for any application that would like to store  persistent collections . The  z/TPFCS database  handles collection sizes from 1 element to more than 2000000000 elements.
Z – glossary entries
z/TPFCS  primary record   The first logical copy of each record used to represent a collection. If a collection is not shadowed,  z/TPF collection support  ( z/TPFCS ) then uses only primary records to represent the collection. 
 
 z/TPFCS  shadow record   A duplicate copy of each of the records used to represent the  z/TPF collection support  ( z/TPFCS ) collection in the  z/TPF  database.  z/TPFCS  provides shadowing independent of  z/TPF  duplication of files. 
 z/TPFDF   The short name for  z/Transaction Processing Facility Database Facility Enterprise Edition . 
 z/TPFDF collection descriptor   In  z/TPF support for MongoDB , a file that describes the mapping of a  z/TPFDF  file to an XML format that can be used by the  z/TPF system . This file is initially generated by using the  ZUDFM DESCRIPTOR  command and might be customized by the user. The suffix of this file is  adbi.xml . 
 z/Transaction Processing Facility Database Facility Enterprise Edition   An IBM® licensed program that is a database manager for application programs that run in a  z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition  (commonly referred to as  z/TPF ) environment.

[Rank 2] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition C – glossary entries
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=glossary-c-entries
Score: 0.28882113099098206
Content: C – glossary entries
CodesetRegistry-CodesetEncoding name   A code page number might be 500 or 1047.  IBM will give it a name such as IBM-500 or IBM-1047.  Names prefixed with  IBM-  are supported by IBM. 
 collapsed I-stream   An I-stream that completes the transition from an in-use I-stream to a parked or fenced I-stream. See also  in-use I-stream ,  parked I-stream , and  fenced I-stream .  
 collection   The primary entity in  z/TPF collection support  ( z/TPFCS ). A collection consists of a related group of elements organized within a data store. Collections are created by applications and can be temporary or persistent. 
 collection part objects   In  z/TPF collection support  ( z/TPFCS ), objects used to represent the same collection that are unrelated in terms of inheritance. 
 collection parts   See  collection part objects . 
 column   A vertical arrangement of information in a table. 
 command   A request to perform an operation or run a program.  When parameters, arguments, flags, or other operands are associated with a command, the resulting character string is a single command. 
 Operator messages, accepted only from CRAS terminals, that are used to communicate with the control program to request services or modify system parameters. They are sometimes called functional messages or Z-messages because the first character of the message is always Z. 
 command file   A file containing commands to run in sequence.  
 commit   In  z/TPF transaction services , to apply all of the file changes that were made inside of a commit scope. 
 commit scope   A unit of work that groups together a set of database updates. 
 common block   A  z/TPF  block that is allocated within a common frame. A common block is visible to all  entry control block s ( ECB s) at the same address. 
 common deployment   A mechanism to make  deployment descriptors  available for use.
C – glossary entries
common deployment   A mechanism to make  deployment descriptors  available for use. 
 common deployment configuration file   A file that contains information about each function or component that uses  common deployment . 
 common frame   4 KB of storage that are allocated in the pool of storage that is visible to all  entry control block s ( ECB s) at the same address. 
 common frame control table (CCT)   A control table that keeps track of which common frames are in use, what block type they are being used for, and the  entry control block  ( ECB ) that obtained the block. 
 common I⁄O (CIO)   A  z/TPF  control program routine that manages  input/output  (I⁄O) operations through a macro interface that permits the set of CIO macros supporting each I⁄O function to make use of a centralized service structure. 
 common I⁄O handler   The first-level   input/output  (I⁄O) interrupt handler.  It saves the current environment, passes control to the appropriate device handler, and performs I⁄O initiation in response to requests from the control program. 
 COMM SOURCE   Communication source program. 
 common symbol table   In  expression enhancements for the z/TPF debugger , a table that contains symbols that are considered common to real-time assembler programs. Use of the common symbol table eliminates the need for multiple copies of the DSECT and symbol information for each real-time assembler program being retained and loaded to the  z/TPF system . Instead, only one copy of the common DSECTs or symbols is kept in the  z/TPF system . You use the common symbol table user exit (UCST) to add the DSECTs and symbols to the table. 
 communication domain   A name space or an address space that shares common communication properties, such as naming conventions and protocol address formats. 
 communication source program (COMM SOURCE)   The first  entry control block  ( ECB )-controlled program to be given control for routing input messages to the intended destination.

[Rank 1] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition Additional considerations when using B+Tree indexing
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=indexing-additional-considerations-when-using-btree
Score: 0.24745501577854156
Content: Additional considerations when using  B + Tree  indexing     If you use  B + Tree  indexing support, keep the following points in mind:     The key fields are defined by the default keys in the DBDEF. 
 
 B + Tree  files are intended to be used for files with one set of default keys (that is, one primary key).  If multiple default keys are defined (one set for each primary key), the organization of the first default key is used to organize the  B + Tree  index. 
 Note:  If a file has multiple default keys, the layout (organization, displacement, and length) of the remaining default keys must match the layout (organization, displacement, and length) of the first default key up to the number of keys in the first default key.   
 The sum of all keys, including the primary key, must be unique. Individual keys do not have to be unique. For example, in  Figure 1 , there is more than one LREC with a salary of $90000 but only one with a salary of $90000 and the name ADAMS. 
 Each subfile has its own  B + Tree  index. For example, a file using algorithm #TPFDB01 (26 subfiles) would have 26 separate  B + Tree  structures. 
 More than one file can use the same  B + Tree  index file DSECT. Each file contains its own  B + Tree  index structure. In other words, several data files can have a DBDEF statement referring to the same  B + Tree  index DBDEF (for example, NODEID=B070). 
 Packing a  B + Tree  data file builds or rebuilds the  B + Tree  index structure unless the file contains only a prime block with no overflow blocks. 
 Packing a  B + Tree  file must be enforced by specifying the  PACK  parameter on the  DBCLS  macro or the  DFCLS_PACK  value on the  dfcls  function.
Additional considerations when using B+Tree indexing
Packing a  B + Tree  file must be enforced by specifying the  PACK  parameter on the  DBCLS  macro or the  DFCLS_PACK  value on the  dfcls  function. 
 
 CRUISE  capture processing on a  B + Tree  subfile does not capture the  B + Tree  nodes.  CRUISE  restore processing on a  B + Tree  subfile releases the node blocks in the existing  B + Tree  index, but does not rebuild the  B + Tree  index. That is, restore processing leaves the  B + Tree  data subfiles without a  B + Tree  index. You must pack restored subfiles (either by using the  CRUISE  or ZUDFM utilities, or by using a close pack API in an application) to rebuild the  B + Tree  index. If you do not rebuild the  B + Tree  index, there might be a performance impact because there is no  B + Tree  index available and subfiles must be searched sequentially. 
 If a file is changed from block indexing to  B + Tree  indexing, existing TLRECs of the block index file are deleted when the file is packed. 
 
 B + Tree  indexing does not support extended LRECs. 
 Each  B + Tree  node block must be large enough to contain at least four TLRECs. 
 The number of TLRECs that can fit into a node block depends on the size of the blocks and the size of the keys that are used. Because each node header file is 26 bytes, and each TLREC uses 8 bytes in addition to the key size, use the following formula to calculate the number of TLRECs that will be in your node blocks.   Number of TLRECs   =   (block size - 26) / (8 + key size) 
 
 If you convert an existing file to allow it to use  B + Tree  indexing, reassemble any assembler applications that use it, to flag any incompatible options. Applications that assemble cleanly do not have to be reloaded. 
 Never pack a  B + Tree  index file.
Additional considerations when using B+Tree indexing
Never pack a  B + Tree  index file. 
 If a  B + Tree  file  is converted to a non- B + Tree  file, the nodes will be reported lost when recoup  is run. Use the  CRUISE  PACK function to remove the node file references from the headers of the subfiles. You must remove the old node file references if you intend to convert the file into a  B + Tree  file again. 
 When you use the  CRUISE  PACK or CAPTURE functions, you must specify a DBDEF file version that uses single ECB chain chasing. Consider using a DBDEF file version that uses multiple ECB chain chasing for recoup or CRUISE VERIFY functions.

[Rank 2] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition B+Tree indexing
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=indexing-btree
Score: 0.24051904678344727
Content: B + Tree  indexing     B + Tree  indexing is a method of accessing and maintaining data. It should be used for large files that have unusual, unknown, or changing distributions because it reduces I/O processing when files are read. Also consider  B + Tree  indexing for files with long overflow chains. 
 
 Note:  Unlike block indexing, where the number of I/Os can increase substantially as the file gets larger, the number of I/Os using  B + Tree  indexing remains minimal regardless of the size of the file.   A  B + Tree  file consists of a data file, which contains logical records (LRECs), and an index file, which contains technical logical records (TLRECs). The  B + Tree  index file, which consists of blocks (also called nodes), is maintained internally by the  z/TPFDF product . The index file has its own file ID, DSECT, and DBDEF statements. The prime block of the  B + Tree  index file (also called the root node) is pointed to by the header in the prime block of the  B + Tree  data file. 
 
 B + Tree  indexing is similar to block indexing but has the following advantages:     Dynamically updates TLRECs 
 Has an unlimited number of TLRECs 
 Can use mixed key organization for file operations 
 Is used for all LREC searches when the specified keys entirely or partially match the default keys in the DBDEF statement. 
   
 Note:     If the distribution of overflows can be predicted, you may want to use an algorithm. A well-distributed algorithm that has one or two overflows for each subfile will probably outperform a  B + Tree  index. 
 You can define a file to use an algorithm and  B + Tree  indexing. The algorithm accesses the subfile and  B + Tree  indexing accesses the record in the subfile. 
             
 B+Tree index file node blocks   B + Tree  index file node blocks contain TLRECs that contain file addresses of the blocks at a lower level of a file. Those lower-level blocks might be other node blocks or data blocks.

[Rank 3] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition B+Tree index support
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=subfiles-btree-index-support
Score: 0.15634815394878387
Content: B + Tree  index support     B + Tree  index support is similar to block index support. Like block indexing,  B + Tree  index support uses index LRECs (also known as technical LRECs or TLRECs) to identify the first data LREC contained in each block of a subfile. Unlike block indexing, these TLRECs are not maintained in the prime block of the subfile. Instead, these TLRECs are maintained in a separate  B + Tree  structure. 
 Instead of reading all the LRECs in a subfile until it locates the desired LREC,  z/TPFDF  can go directly from the  B + Tree  structure to the block containing the requested LREC. LRECs are then searched sequentially in that block. 
 The  B + Tree  structure, maintained by  z/TPFDF , is transparent to the application program. The database administrator must specify that a file is using  B + Tree  indexing in the DSECT and DBDEF statements.  z/TPFDF  then maintains technical logical records (TLRECs) in the  B + Tree  structure associated with the subfile. Every TLREC in the lowest level of the  B + Tree  structure points to a data block of the subfile. 
 For more information about  B + Tree  indexing, see   z/TPFDF Database Administration .

[Rank 4] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition B+Tree index file node blocks
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=indexing-btree-index-file-node-blocks
Score: 0.15280596911907196
Content: B + Tree  index file node blocks   
 B + Tree  index file node blocks contain TLRECs that contain file addresses of the blocks at a lower level of a file. Those lower-level blocks might be other node blocks or data blocks.  
 TLRECs in node blocks have the following layout:     Size of the TLREC (2 bytes). 
 Primary key (1 byte).     Key 03 for a node pointing to another node 
 Key 04 for a node pointing to a data block. 
   
 File address of the lower-level node or data block (4 bytes or 8 bytes). 
 Record code check (RCC) equal to X'00' for leaf nodes, or the last byte of the data file ID for nonleaf nodes (1 byte).  
 The concatenation of the primary key and its associated default keys found in the DBDEF of the data file. These keys point to the first TLREC of a child node or the first LREC of a block in the  B + Tree  data file. 
     
 Additional information   
 B + Tree  node blocks cannot be migrated to use FARF6 addresses. In the DBDEF macro, the  F6PRP  and  F6OFP  parameters (OP5 bits 3 and 4 must be off) must be set to the  NO  value (the default) for  B + Tree  node files. FARF6 addresses can be used in  B + Tree  node blocks for new  B + Tree  databases by setting the  F6HDR  parameter to the  YES  value and the  PF0  parameter to the  LD6  or  SS6  value. 
 The header format for a  B + Tree  node (index) file must match the header format for the associated data file (that is, the F6HDR DBDEF parameter must be set to the same value). However, the actual pool types dispensed (PF0 parameter) may be different in the data and node files. 
 The key information is stored contiguously in the technical LREC, but the keys do not have to be stored contiguously in the data LRECs.
#

Content: B + Tree  data file characteristics     To use  B + Tree  indexing, set the DBDEF macro parameters, equivalent DSECT parameters, or equivalent default values for a  B + Tree  data file as follows:     OP1 bits 2, 3, and 6 must be off. 
 OP3 bit 5 must be on. 
 
 B + Tree  data files cannot be migrated to use FARF6 addresses. FARF6 addresses can be used in new  B + Tree  databases. 
 The header format for a  B + Tree  data file must match the header format for the associated node (index) file (that is, the F6HDR DBDEF parameter must be set to the same value). However, the actual pool types dispensed (PF0 parameter) may be different in the data and node files. 
 The RBV algorithm value cannot be #TPFDB0D. 
 The TQK value must be greater than 4. 
 If present, the PIN value must be less than or equal to 50. 
 The TYP value must be R. 
 The NOC variable cannot be present. 
 The SKE variable cannot be present. 
 The NLR variable cannot be present. 
     Also, the  B + Tree  data file DBDEF must have the following parameter settings:    A  PKY  statement to define default keys 
 
 NODEID= fileid  (where  fileid  is the &SW00WID value shown in the associated  B + Tree  index file) 
 KEYCHECK=YES 
 UNIQUE=YES 
 
 DELEMPTY=YES  and  FULLBCH=YES If  DELEMPTY=YES  and  FULLBCH=YES  are not specified, you might have a significant number of blocks in the  B + Tree  data file that are empty, which can result in performance issues. Additionally, if these parameters are not specified, you cannot use or easily switch an existing database to use multiple ECB chain chasing. For more information about multiple ECB chain chasing, see  Chain chasing B+Tree structures .

Answer: B+Tree データベースにアクセスするときに、空きブロックが多数あり、遅延が発生するのは、主に以下の理由です。  
1. **TLREC の最小数要件**: 各 B+Tree ノード ブロックは少なくとも四つの TLREC を含む必要があります。このため、キーのサイズが大きい場合やブロック サイズが小さい場合、一つのノード ブロックに収まる TLREC の数が減少し、ノード ブロックが空き状態となってしまいます。  
2. **キーの分布**: キーの分布が不均衡であると、特定のノードに多くの TLREC が集中し、他のノードが空き状態となることがあります。これにより、検索時に不要な I/O が発生し、遅延が生じます。  
3. **DELEMPTY および FULLBCH パラメータの設定**: DBDEF で DELEMPTY=YES および FULLBCH=YES を指定しないと、空きブロックが多数残り、パフォーマンスに影響を与えます。これらのパラメータが適切に設定されていないと、既存のデータベースを複数 ECB 鎖探索に切り替えるのが難しくなります。  
これらの要因が組み合わさることで、B+Tree データベースへのアクセス時に空きブロックが多数あり、遅延が発生することになります。

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/cics-ts/6.x?topic=codes-asp1
Score: 0.12697023153305054
Content: ASP1       

Explanation    Intersystem communication failed while a syncpoint was being taken. Communication with the coordinator system has been interrupted, and the failure occurred during the critical indoubt period of syncpoint processing. As a result this CICS system is in doubt about the outcome of the unit of work for the transaction. 
 Alternatively, a transaction may have timed out while waiting for Recoverable Resource Management Services (RRMS) to provide the outcome of the unit of work, or RRMS may have failed during the critical indoubt period. 
 The transaction definition specifies WAIT(YES) as an indoubt attribute. Therefore the unit of work is not completed but is shunted and allowed to wait for resynchronization with the coordinator system. If the WAITTIME attribute is specified on the transaction definition, the unit of work waits for the specified time. If after that time the coordinator system has not resynchronized, a unilateral decision is made about the unit of work as specified by the ACTION keyword on the transaction definition. A WAITTIME of zero, the default, means an indefinite wait. The unit of work can also be forced to take a unilateral decision by means of a CEMT SET UOW command. 
   

System action    The transaction is abnormally terminated. The EXEC CICS HANDLE ABEND command cannot handle this abend. 
 The associated unit of work is shunted awaiting the return of the coordinator system. Recoverable resources updated by the unit of work remain locked. The locks are released when the unit of work is backed out or committed at resynchronization time, or when a unilateral decision is made by this system. 
 Message DFHAC2201 is sent to the terminal end user if possible, and message DFHAC2231 is sent to transient data destination CSMT.
ASP1
User response    None. Any updates performed by the unit of work are resolved automatically when resynchronization with the coordinator system takes place. 
 Alternatively, the user can force resolution of the updates independently of the coordinator system by making a CEMT request to commit or back out the unit of work.

Content: CMPR2     When the program is called for the first time, the PERFORM statement will be executed. If the  N > 1  test succeeds, the program will return to the calling program. 
 However, this means that the PERFORM statement has not reached normal completion because paragraph A never returned to the point from which it was performed. The compiler-generated mechanism at the end of paragraph A is still "set" to return back to the PERFORM statement. 
 Thus, on the second call to the program, the ELSE path will be taken, 1 will be subtracted from N, and control will be transferred by the GO TO statement to paragraph A. However, if the test  N > 1  fails, the PERFORM mechanism is still set. So, when the end of paragraph A is reached, instead of falling through into paragraph B, control is "returned" to the MOVE statement after the PERFORM statement. 
 These results might not be intended. The problem might occur whenever all of the following conditions occur: 
   The program returns to the calling program with an EXIT PROGRAM or GOBACK statement. 
 A PERFORM statement performs a paragraph or a range of paragraphs, and those paragraphs might also be reached by a GO TO statement or by falling through into the paragraph. 
 All such PERFORM statements have not had a chance to return prior to the execution of the EXIT PROGRAM or GOBACK statement.

Content: z/TPF file system support     The  z/TPF system  provides support for the following  file system s:     
 z/TPF collection support file system (TFS)   TFS  provides support for a subsystem-unique, processor-shared  file system  that is maintained across processor IPLs. 
 TFS  uses  z/TPF collection support  as its storage mechanism; therefore, files in  TFS  cannot be created, updated, or deleted unless  get file storage  ( GFS ) is active. 
 TFS  does not use the  atime  (access time) or  ctime  (change time) time stamp; however, you can set the access time by using the  utime  function. 
 
 
 Memory file system (MFS)   MFS  provides support for a subsystem-unique, processor-unique  file system  that is not maintained across processor IPLs and is reinitialized every time it is mounted. 
 MFS  uses system heap as its storage mechanism; therefore, it is a substantially faster  file system  than the  TFS .  Furthermore, because  MFS  stores files in  system heap storage , those files can be created, updated, and deleted in any  z/TPF system  state. 
 
 
 Fixed file system (FFS)   FFS  provides support for a processor-unique  file system  that is built by using a subsystem-unique, processor-shared fixed file record type; that is, only one processor can mount an  FFS  in read/write mode at one time, but multiple processors can mount the same  FFS  in read/only mode. The  file system  supports record buffering, i-node and directory caching, file and byte locking, and user-named attributes for files. 
 The  file system  uses core locking to serialize write access to the file. By being able to mount the  file system  on multiple processors in read/only mode, dirty reading can be done; however, if your application reads data from a file that is not locked, that data might change after the read.
z/TPF file system support
FFS  uses fixed file records for both i-nodes and data records; therefore,  FFS  provides a  file system  for files that need to be maintained across system IPLs where performance is more important than minimizing the use of file space, and where data must not be exposed to corruption that might be caused by applications inadvertently overwriting pool records. 
 
 
 Pool file system (PFS)   PFS  provides support for a processor-unique  file system  that is built by using a subsystem-unique, processor-shared fixed file record type for i-nodes and pool records for data; that is, only one processor can mount an  PFS  in read/write mode at one time, but multiple processors can mount the same  PFS  in read/only mode. The  file system  supports record buffering, i-node and directory caching, file and byte locking, and user named-attributes for files. 
 The  file system  uses core locking to serialize write access to the file. By being able to mount the  file system  on multiple processors in read/only mode, dirty reading can be done; however, if your application reads data from a file that is not locked, that data might change after the read. 
 PFS  uses fixed file records for i-nodes and pool records for data records; therefore,  PFS  provides a  file system  for files that need to be maintained across system IPLs with a high level of performance but by using pool records for data provides a more efficient use of file space.

Figure 1.  z/TPF   file system s     File ownership and accessibility in the  file system  are controlled by using the  POSIX -compliant structures of user ID, group ID, and access permissions associated with each file in the  file system . Application programs can interact with the  file system  through  file system  C functions. 
 You also can use the following commands to manage the  file system :    The ZAVFS and ZDVFS commands allow you to change and display  file system  configuration and trace information. 
 The ZFILE commands are a set of commands that allow you to work with and manage files on the  file system . 
 The ZOVFS and ZPVFS commands provide  file system security  and allow you to control who can work with files on the  file system . 
 The ZFILE pax and ZFILE tar commands allow you to archive and restore files from one  z/TPF system  to another and between a UNIX or  Linux®  system and a  z/TPF system . 
     To use  z/TPF file system support , you must initialize the  z/TPF collection support file system (TFS) ; see  Initializing the z/TPF collection support file system  for more information. If the TFS is already initialized, but you need to increase the number of file system records, or if you need to increase the size of the  PFS  or the  FFS , see  Increasing the number of file system records .

Manage file system mount points  The  z/TPF system  uses a number of directories as mount points for the file system. For some of these directories, you must mount a  specific file system on that directory to enable a particular z/TPF capability. Content: z/TPF  file system     The  z/TPF   file system  automatically and transparently handles low-level problems such as record blocking, allocation, chaining, and locking protocols. The  z/TPF   file system  also gives efficient direct access to data in a file. When used appropriately, the hierarchical file system can significantly reduce the cost and time required to design, implement, and maintain applications. 
 The  z/TPF   file system   application programming interface  (APIs) include all of the ANSI Standard C library (ISO/IEC 9899-1990, section 7) and most of the  POSIX 1, standards sections 5 and 6. The  z/TPF   file system  is  not  POSIX compliant but for most of the API functions, the interfaces and semantics are identical to  POSIX 1 (see the   z/TPF C/C++ Language Support User's Guide  for details about deviations between the  z/TPF   file system  APIs and the POSIX.1 standards). 
 The  z/TPF   file system  APIs work at two levels:     Buffered I/O 
 System-level I/O.
z/TPF file system
The  z/TPF   file system  APIs work at two levels:     Buffered I/O 
 System-level I/O. 
   The more abstract level is the buffered I/O functions, declared in < stdio.h >. The buffered I/O functions operate on a pointer to  FILE . Examples include  fopen ,  fclose  and  fflush ;  fread  and  fwrite ; the formatted I/O functions such as  fprintf  and  fscanf ; the character I/O functions such as  fgetc ,  fgets ,  fputc ,  fputs ; and many others. These APIs are typically used in C language applications that need to create and access files. In general, they are easier to use and more efficient than the less abstract system-level functions that follow.   The system-level I/O functions, declared in < unistd.h >, < fcntl.h >, < dir.h >, and other headers, are appropriate in cases where an application needs to work on the directory structure itself or where more control over files than is provided by the buffered I/O functions is required. The system-level I/O functions operate on a file descriptor, a path name (which is a C string), or a pointer to  DIR . Examples include  creat ,  open ,  close ,  read ,  write ,  fcntl ,  chdir ,  chown ,  chmod ,  mkdir ,  mknod , and  stat , and many others. 
 It is possible to switch levels if necessary. The  fileno  function returns the file descriptor underlying a pointer to  FILE , allowing you to switch from buffered I/O to system-level I/O. Conversely, the  fdopen  function creates a pointer to  FILE  from a previously opened file descriptor, allowing you to switch from system-level I/O to buffered I/O.

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/open-xl-c-cpp-zos/2.2.0?topic=new-compiler-options
Score: 0.12410371750593185
Content: Compiler options     
 Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS®  introduced support for the following compiler options:   
 -gdwarf-4, -gdwarf-5 : Specifies the version of DWARF for the debug information. 
 
 -gsplit-dwarf : Enables generating debug information into a separate file. 
 
 -march=arch15, -march=z17 : Supports the latest  IBM    z17®  architecture to reduce CPU utilization and operating costs. 
 
 -mzos-cics : Enables CICS integrated translator. 
 
 -mzos-hlq-cics : Specifies the HLQ for CICS libraries. 
 
 -mzos-ims : Generates object code to run under the Information Management System (IMS) subsystem. 
 
 -mzos-listing-file-name : Specifies the file name to use for the listing file. 
 
 -mzos-listing=json : Enables the creation of a listing file in JSON format. 
 
 -mzos-plist : Specifies how arguments are passed to  main() . 
     
 Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS  introduced support for the following Clang options:   -faligned-allocation 
 -fclang-abi-compat 
 -fdump-record-layouts 
 -ffast-math, -fno-fast-math 
 -fno-strict-overflow 
 -fwrapv-pointer 
 -fwrapv 
 -mbackchain 
     For more information about these options, see  Compiler options  in the  Compiler Reference .
#


[Rank 3] Title: IBM Open XL C/C++ for z/OS Source compatibility
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/open-xl-c-cpp-zos/2.2.0?topic=guide-source-compatibility
Score: 0.07288292050361633
Content: Source compatibility     The following migration concerns have been identified for the transition from  Open XL C/C++ 2.1 for z/OS®  to  Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS : 
 

Type based aliasing improvements    When accessing pointer types, by default,  Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS  now generates distinct type‑based alias analysis (TBAA) tags for incompatible pointers, enabling effective alias analysis. This change alters the behavior of the code that contains strict‑aliasing violations. The new default can be disabled with  -fno-pointer-tbaa  option.
Source compatibility
Handling undefined behavior from pointer addition overflow    The  Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS  optimizer is more aggressive, which might expose incorrect behavior on your source code, that might have worked with prior  Open XL C/C++ for z/OS  releases. For example, an expression such as ptr + unsigned_offset < ptr is now optimized to  false , as  ptr + unsigned_offset  will cause undefined behavior if it overflows (or advances past the end of the object).   In  Open XL C/C++ 2.1 for z/OS ,  ptr + unsigned_offset  was optimized to  (ssize_t)unsigned_offset <
0 . This also produces an incorrect overflow check, but the error is less apparent when testing only with pointers located in the low half of the address space. 
 To avoid pointer‑addition overflow, you can perform the addition on integers, for example, use  (uintptr_t)ptr + unsigned_offset < (uintptr_t)ptr . You can also simplify the check by comparing only the offset. For example, replace ptr + offset < end_ptr && ptr + offset >= ptr with  offset < (uintptr_t)(end_ptr - ptr) 
   You can use  -fno‑strict‑overflow  option to enable a language dialect with well‑defined signed‑integer and pointer overflow. In  Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS , the  -fwrapv‑pointer  option makes only pointer overflow well‑defined, leaving signed‑integer overflow unchanged. 
 The  -fwrapv  option now makes only signed‑integer overflow well‑defined, without affecting pointer overflow. The pointer overflow is controlled by the new  -fwrapv-pointer  option. The  -fno‑strict‑overflow  flag implicitly enables both  -fwrapv  and  -fwrapv-pointer , preserving its original behavior. 
   

Clang compiler option change: -Ofast to -O3 -ffast-math    Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS  has deprecated the  -Ofast  compiler option. The  -Ofast  option is a shorthand for the  -O3 -ffast-math  options. Any use of the  ‑Ofast  option with  Open XL C/C++ 2.1 for z/OS  or earlier needs to be migrated to  ‑O3 ‑ffast-math  option.
#

Content: Supported language standards     Open XL C/C++ 2.2 for z/OS®  is designed to support the following standards and specifications. You can refer to these standards and specifications for precise definitions of some of the features found in this information. For more information, see  International Organization for Standardization (ISO) . 
   The C language is consistent with  Programming languages - C ISO/IEC 9899:1999  (C99) and a subset of  Programming languages - C ISO/IEC 9899:2011  (C11)  and  Information Technology - Programming languages - C, ISO/IEC 9899:2018  (C17/C18).   
 The C++ language is consistent with  Programming languages - C++ ISO/IEC 14882:1998  (C++98),  Programming languages - C++ ISO/IEC 14882:2003(E)  (C++03), a subset of  Programming languages - C++ ISO/IEC 14882:2011  (C++11),  Programming languages - C++ (ISO/IEC 14882:2014)  (C++14),  Programming languages - C++ (ISO/IEC 14882:2017)  (C++17) ,  and  Programming languages - C++ (ISO/IEC 14882:2025)  (C++20) . 
   The following standards are supported in combination with the z/OS UNIX System Services element: 
   A subset of  IEEE Std. 1003.1-2001 (Single UNIX Specification, Version 3) . For more information, see  IEEE . 
 
 IEEE Std 1003.1—1990, IEEE Standard Information Technology—Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX)—Part 1: System Application Program Interface (API) [C language] , copyright 1990 by the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers, Inc. 
 The core features of  IEEE P1003.1a Draft 6 July 1991, Draft Revision to Information Technology—Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX), Part 1: System Application Program Interface (API) [C Language] , copyright 1992 by the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers, Inc. 
 
 IEEE Std 1003.2—1992, IEEE Standard Information Technology—Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX)—Part 2: Shells and Utilities , copyright 1990 by the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers, Inc.
Supported language standards
The core features of  IEEE Std P1003.4a/D6—1992, IEEE Draft Standard Information Technology—Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX)—Part 1: System Application Program Interface (API)—Amendment 2: Threads Extension [C language] , copyright 1990 by the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers, Inc. 
 The core features of  IEEE 754-1985 (R1990) IEEE Standard for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic (ANSI) , copyright 1985 by the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers, Inc. 
 
 X/Open CAE Specification, System Interfaces and Headers, Issue 4 Version 2 , copyright 1994 by The Open Group 
 
 X/Open CAE Specification, Networking Services, Issue 4 , copyright 1994 by The Open Group 
 United States Government's  Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) publication for the programming language C, FIPS-160 , issued by National Institute of Standards and Technology, 1991

Content: Require Response   
 If you select true in the Require Response listbox (the default is false) then:  
 The macro runtime displays the text string  (required)  to the right of the input field, to indicate to the end user that input is required for this input field. 
 The macro runtime disables the OK button of the prompt window until the input field of the prompt window contains text.   
 The input field can contain text either because you have specified a Default Response or because the user has typed text into the input field. 
 When OK is enabled, the end user can click either OK or Cancel, as usual:  
 Clicking OK causes the macro to process the Prompt action and continue processing the macro. 
 Clicking Cancel terminates the macro playback. 
   
 When OK is not enabled, the end user can click Cancel.  
 Clicking Cancel terminates the macro playback. 
   
   
  Thus, setting Require Response to true has the effects of reminding the end user  (by displaying  (required)  to the right of the input field) that a response is required before proceeding, and of requiring the end user to enter text in the input field before clicking OK (by disabling OK until the input field contains text). However, if the Prompt action contains a Default Response, then OK is enabled and the default response is displayed in the input field.   If you select false in the Require Response listbox then:  
 The macro runtime does not display  the text string  (required) to the right of the input field. 
 The macro runtime enables the OK button on the prompt window immediately as soon as the prompt window is displayed, whether or not the input field contains text.  
 The user can click OK or Cancel, as usual:  
 Clicking OK causes the macro runtime to process the Prompt action and then to continue processing the macro. In the Prompt action, if the input field is blank, the macro runtime does not send an input key sequence to session window. 
 Clicking Cancel terminates the macro playback.
Require Response
Clicking Cancel terminates the macro playback. 
   
   
  Thus, setting Require Response to false has the effect of allowing the user to continue processing the macro by clicking OK, even if the input field of the prompt is blank.   If the  promptall  attribute of the <HAScript> element (or of the <actions> element) is set to true, and you have several prompt actions in the macro (or in the macro screen) with Require Response set to true, then at the start of macro playback (or at the start of the playback of the macro screen),  when the macro runtime displays all the prompt input fields in a single prompt window, the macro runtime does not enable the OK button in the prompt window until all required input fields contain text (see  The promptall attributes  ).

Content: ADCNC     

Purpose    Use the ADCNC statement when defining conditional dependencies for an operation, to specify a condition. 
   

Format    
1  ADCNC?  ACTION (
2.1! ADD
2.1 SETDEFAULT
1 )  CONDID (
2.1  condition ID 
1 )  CONDDEPNO (
2.1  number of condition dependency 
1 )?  CONDCOUNT (
2.1! 0
2.1  condition counter 
1 )?  CONDDESCR ('
2.1  descriptive text 
1 ')     

Restrictions    You cannot use ACTION(SETDEFAULT) to set default values for the following keywords:    CONDID 
 CONDDEPNO 
 
     

Parameters        ACTION ( SETDEFAULT  |  ADD )   If you specify SETDEFAULT, all the other values that you set in the ADCNC statement become the default values for all the ADCNC statements that follow. The application description database is not updated. The parameters that you do not set, are assigned their standard defaults.   If you specify ADD or use it by default, the statement can result in an update of the database. 
 
 CONDID( condition ID )   Condition identifier. Valid values are from 1 to 999. 
 CONDDEPNO( number of condition dependencies )   Number of condition dependencies to be included in this condition, each one corresponding to an ADCNS statement. 
 CONDCOUNT( condition counter  |  0 )   Condition counter. Use it to define the rule type:     0   All the condition dependencies in this condition must be true. 
 n   At least  n  out of the condition dependencies in this condition must be true. 
 
 
 CONDDESCR( 'descriptive text' )   A free-format description of the condition. It can be up to 16 characters and must be contained within single quotation marks. Do not include delimiters, such as parentheses and single quotation marks, in the description. 
 
     
 

Examples    This example defines a condition including two condition dependencies: 
 ADCNC   CONDID(  3) CONDDEPNO(2) CONDCOUNT(1)
        CONDDESCR('WITH 2 COND.DEPS') 
ADCNS …
ADCNS …
