Answer: DBB Migrationツールはどうやって使えばいいですか？  
DBB Migration ツールを使用するには、以下の手順に従ってください。  

1. **準備**: マイグレーション先のローカル Git リポジトリ（z/OS UNIX システム上）が事前に作成されていることを確認します。  
2. **コマンド実行**: DBB Migration ツールは、SMP/e によってインストールされた Dependency Based Build（DBB）のインストールディレクトリ内の `migration/bin` ディレクトリに配置されています。通常のパスは `/usr/lpp/IBM/dbb/migration/bin` です。このディレクトリ内の `migrate.sh` スクリプトを実行します。  
   ```sh
   $DBB_HOME/migration/bin/migrate.sh -r /u/ユーザー名/マイグレーション -m マッピングルール ソース
   ```  
   例えば、デフォルト設定で `MIGRATE.TECHDOC.SOURCE` PDS のすべてのメンバーを `/u/user1/Migration` にマイグレートする場合：  
   ```sh
   $DBB_HOME/migration/bin/migrate.sh -r /u/user1/Migration -m Mapping Rule[hlq:MIGRATE.TECHDOC,extension:SRC, toLower:true] SOURCE
   ```  
3. **コードページ変換**: ツールは、z/OS コードページから Git で使用するエンコーディングに必要な変換を自動的に行います。  
4. **.gitattributes の作成/更新**: 必要に応じて、`.gitattributes` ファイルに適切なエンコーディングマッピングを設定します。  
5. **コミットとプッシュ**: マイグレーション後、ローカル Git リポジトリにコミットし、選択したリモート Git サーバーにプッシュします。  

詳細な設定やオプションについては、[IBM Documentation サイト](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ibm-z-devops-guide?topic=git-db) を参照してください。

Git for source code management
Git basics      Git is a distributed "version control system" for source code. It provides many features to allow developers to check in and check out code with a full history and audit trail for all changes. 
 Source is stored in repositories (also known as "repos") on hierarchical file systems on Linux®, MacOS, Windows, or z/OS UNIX System Services. 
 The team stores a primary copy of the repository on a service running Git on a server (see  Common Git provider options ). Such services provide all the resilience required to safeguard the code and its history. Once source code is moved into a repository on the server, that becomes the primary source of truth, so existing processes to ensure the resilience of copies on z/OS are no longer required. 
 An application repo can be cloned from the team's chosen Git server (known as the "remote") to any machine that has Git, including a developer's local computer using popular integrated development environments (IDEs) such as IBM® Developer for z/OS (IDz) and Microsoft’s Visual Studio Code (VS Code). By default, clones contain all the files and folders in the repository, as well as their complete version histories. (Cloning provides many options to select what is copied and synchronized.) 
 All Git operations that transfer the data held in the repository ( clone ,  push ,  fetch , and  pull ) use SSH or HTTPS secure communications. Pros and cons of each protocol are discussed in ["Git on the Server - The Protocols"](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-on-the-Server-The-Protocols). 
   NOTE:  SSH on z/OS 
 z/OS UNIX System Services includes [OpenSSH](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/3.1.0?topic=zbed-zos-openssh). z/OS OpenSSH provides the following z/OS extensions: 
   System Authorization Facility (SAF) key ring: z/OS OpenSSH can be configured to allow z/OS OpenSSH keys to be stored in SAF key rings.

Git workflow by role      To begin using the software development lifecycle with Git for an existing z/OS application, the source of the application must already be located in a Git repository. For information on how to migrate source files from z/OS to Git, see  Migrating data from z/OS to Git . 
 Once the source code of the application is in a Git repository, the workflow involves tasks that use Git capabilities such as cloning, pulling, branching, committing, pushing, and merging. 
 The following diagram summarizes the Git workflow by role at a high level.    
 
 Note:   The commands mentioned in this section are high-level commands to provide an overall idea of the workflow, and may omit arguments or use sample arguments (enclosed in angle brackets; for example,  <sample-argument> ) for clarity.         Developing new features or bug fixes : Upon receiving a new assignment, a developer performs the following tasks: 
     Clones or pulls the latest source files from the central Git repository to their local repository using the following commands: 
     If cloning the repository for the first time: 
 git clone <repo-url> 
   
   If working on an existing cloned repository: 
 git pull 
   
   
   Works on their code changes using a dedicated feature branch, which can be created using the following command: 
 git switch -c <feature>
   
   Commits and pushes the changes to their feature branch on the central Git repository using the following commands: 
 git commit
git push
   When using the  git commit  command, adding a descriptive, concise commit message with the  -m
<'msg'>  option can help the both the developer and their team understand the changes in the commit when reviewing the code. 
 
   Starts the merge workflow from their feature branch to the  main  branch. 
 It is recommended to create a peer review request (for example, a pull request or a merge request) during this stage.
Git for source code management
It is recommended to create a peer review request (for example, a pull request or a merge request) during this stage. 
 
   
     Reviewing the peer review request : The development team or the team lead reviews the request. The request is either approved and merged, or rejected. 
 
     Publishing the release : The release manager creates the release from the  main  branch. The release can be created via a Git provider, or by using the command line. 
 With the command line approach, the following command can be used: 
 git tag -a <version> -m <'msg'>
   Publishing the release is done by the release manager or the development team lead.

Sharing code      It is a common practice that mainframe applications share common code. For example, COBOL copybooks are typically shared across applications that process similar data. 
 The following diagram illustrates how teams can define repos to securely share common code. In this example, App Team 1 has common code that App Team 2 can clone and use in their build. 
 Another example (also illustrated in the following diagram) is that an enterprise-wide team can maintain source that is common across many applications. 
     
 Examples of how the z/OS application developer, team lead, and release manager can use Git and other DevOps tools in the larger context of a CI/CD pipeline are outlined in  Role-based usage . See  Git branching model for mainframe development  for detailed guidance on our recommended Git branching model and working practices. 
       

Resources      This page contains reformatted and updated excerpts from [Git training for Mainframers](https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7003251).

Porcelain API    While JGit contains a lot of low level code to work with Git repositories, it also contains a higher level API that mimics some of the Git porcelain commands in the  			 org.eclipse.jgit.api  package.  		 
 Most users of JGit should start here. 
 AddCommand (git-add)   AddCommand allows you to add files to the index and has options available via its setter methods. 
   addFilepattern() 
   Here's a quick example of how to add a set of files to the index using the porcelain API. 
 Git git = new Git(db); AddCommand add = git.add(); add.addFilepattern("someDirectory").call();    CommitCommand (git-commit)   CommitCommand allows you to perform commits and has options available via its setter methods. 
   setAuthor() 
 setCommitter() 
 setAll() 
   Here's a quick example of how to commit using the porcelain API. 
 Git git = new Git(db); CommitCommand commit = git.commit(); commit.setMessage("initial commit").call();    TagCommand (git-tag)   TagCommand supports a variety of tagging options through its setter methods. 
   setName() 
 setMessage() 
 setTagger() 
 setObjectId() 
 setForceUpdate() 
 setSigned() - not supported yet, will throw exception 
   Here's a quick example of how to tag a commit using the porcelain API. 
 Git git = new Git(db); RevCommit commit = git.commit().setMessage("initial commit").call(); RevTag tag = git.tag().setName("tag").call();    LogCommand (git-log)   LogCommand allows you to easily walk a commit graph. 
   add(AnyObjectId start) 
 addRange(AnyObjectId since, AnyObjectId until) 
   Here's a quick example of how get some log messages. 
 Git git = new Git(db); Iterable<RevCommit> log = git.log().call();    MergeCommand (git-merge)   TODO
JGit User Guide - Reference
Ant Tasks    JGit has Ant tasks for some common tasks contained in the  			 org.eclipse.jgit.ant  bundle. 		 
 To use these tasks: 
    <taskdef resource="org/eclipse/jgit/ant/ant-tasks.properties">        <classpath>          <pathelement location="path/to/org.eclipse.jgit.ant-VERSION.jar"/>          <pathelement location="path/to/org.eclipse.jgit-VERSION.jar"/>          <pathelement location="path/to/jsch-0.1.44-1.jar"/>        </classpath>    </taskdef>    This would then provide git-clone, git-init and git-checkout tasks. 
 git-clone      <git-clone uri=" http://egit.eclipse.org/jgit.git " />    The following attributes are required: 
   uri: the uri to clone from 
   The following attributes are optional: 
   dest: the destination to clone to (defaults to use a human readable directory name based on the last path component of the uri) 
 bare: true/false/yes/no to indicate if the cloned repository should be bare or not (defaults to false) 
 branch: the initial branch to check out when cloning the repository (defaults to HEAD) 
   git-init      <git-init />    The following attributes are optional: 
   dest: the path where a git repository is initialized (defaults $GIT_DIR or the current directory) 
 bare: true/false/yes/no to indicate if the repository should be bare or not (defaults to false) 
   git-checkout      <git-checkout src="path/to/repo" branch="origin/experimental" />    The following attributes are required: 
   src: the path to the git repository 
 branch: the initial branch to checkout 
   The following attributes are optional: 
   createbranch: true/false/yes/no to indicate whether the branch should be created if it does not already exist (defaults to false) 
 force: true/false/yes/no: if true/yes and the branch with the given name already exists, the start-point of an existing branch will be set to a new start-point; if false, the existing branch will not be changed (defaults to false) 
   git-add   TODO

Answer: z/OS から Git へソースを移行する手順は 以下 の通りです。  
1. まず、Git リポジトリにソースを移行するため、z/OS 上のアプリケーションのソースが既に Git リポジトリに存在することを確認します。ソースを移行する方法については、「 Migrating data from z/OS to Git 」を参照してください。  
2. ソース コードが Git リポジトリにあることを確認したら、ブランチ作成、コミット、プッシュ、マージなどの Git 機能を使用して開発を行います。  
3. 新しい機能やバグ修正を開発する場合、最新のソース ファイルを中央 Git リポジトリからローカル リポジトリにクローンまたはプルします。  
4. 機能専用のブランチを作成し、変更をコミットして、そのブランチを中央 Git リポジトリにプッシュします。  
5. フィードバック リクエスト（プル リクエストやマージ リクエストなど）を作成して、チームメンバーにレビューを依頼します。  
6. レビューが完了したら、マージを行い、main ブランチに統合します。  
7. リリース マネージャーが main ブランチからリリースを作成し、公開します。  

これにより、z/OS から Git へのソース移行が完了します。

Content: Overview   
 IBM® Enterprise PL/I for z/OS®  is a leading-edge compiler for  IBM z/OS  that helps you create and maintain mission-critical, line-of-business PL/I applications to execute on your z/OS environments. The applications that are created by using  Enterprise PL/I for z/OS  can interoperate with IBM CICS®, IBM Db2®, IBM IMS, and other transactional and data systems. 
 The  Enterprise PL/I for z/OS  compiler can help facilitate your new, business endeavors by helping to integrate PL/I and web-based business processes in web services, XML, Java™, and PL/I applications. This compiler's interoperability helps you capitalize on your existing IT investments while more smoothly incorporating new, web-based applications as part of your organization's infrastructure.
Overview
What's new in Enterprise PL/I for z/OS 6.2    Enterprise PL/I for z/OS 6.2  provides support for the latest  IBM z17  architecture.  
 Enterprise PL/I for z/OS 6.2  introduces the ARCH(15) option allowing you to generate your application code to leverage the latest  IBM z17  hardware architecture. 
 Enterprise PL/I for z/OS 6.2  also offers the following new features and functions: 
   Performance improvements       Use of vector instructions to inline both hex and base64 encoding/decoding 
 Additional inlining of the  REPATTERN  and  VALIDDATE  built-in functions 
   
     New PL/I language enhancements       16-byte integer support 
 New built-in functions to make date-time calculations easier 
   
     New PL/I compiler options       New options to help developers find errors earlier  
   
     Usability enhancements       The compiler flags more code that might cause storage problems 
 Addition of new samples and enhanced documentation 
   
   Enterprise PL/I for z/OS 6.2  reinforces the continuous IBM commitment to the PL/I programming language on the z/OS platform and the continued delivery of new features. 
 With  Enterprise PL/I for z/OS 6.2 , you can take advantage of almost 60 years of IBM experience in PL/I compiler development.

Content: Migrating from Enterprise PL/I V6R1     The 6.1 compiler, like all compilers since 3.9, must be installed in a  PDSE . Also, the  Language Environment  runtime option  XPLINK  must be ON whenever you start the compiler. If you start the compiler under batch by using  IBMZPLI  or under  z/OS UNIX System Services  by using the  pli  command, the compiler itself ensures that it runs with  XPLINK(ON) . However, if you are starting the compiler in some other way, you must ensure that  XPLINK(ON)  is in effect. 
 Enterprise PL/I   6.2  contains some new options, some options with new suboptions, and some options with changed defaults. 
 

New or changed options in Enterprise PL/I 6.1      Existing options with new suboptions     
 
 
 
 
 
     Option   New suboption   
       ARCH    15   
   RULES    NOPUT   
   USAGE   HEXDECODE   
   USAGE    BASE64   
   XINFO   DEFS   
       
 Existing options with changed defaults     
 
 
 
 
 
     Default in 6.2   Default in 6.1   
        JSON(PARSE(v1))   JSON(PARSE(v2))   
       
 Existing options with deleted suboptions     
 
 
 
 
 
     Option   Deleted suboption   
       ARCH    10, 11   
       
 Deleted options       LINECOUNT
Migrating from Enterprise PL/I V6R1
Built-in function changes    Following are the built-in function changes:   
 RAISE2  is no longer supported. 
 
 LOWER2  is no longer supported and has been replaced with ISRA. 
 
 POPCNT  is no longer supported and has been replaced with  IPOPCNT  (which gives the total population count for its argument rather than the population count in each byte or the argument). 
 In the integer manipulation functions, all arguments must now be  REAL FIXED(p,0)  with  q = 0  or  BIT NONVARYING 
 
 Use of  SECS, SECSTODATE, UTCSECS, DAYSTOSECS , and  SECSTODAYS  is now flagged as dangerous with the use of the corresponding  MICROSECS  function recommended instead. 
 
 ROUND(x,n)  of  FIXED(p,q)  is no longer supported if n > q (when the rounding would be too far to the right. For example,  ROUND(x,4)  is not supported if x is  FIXED(15,2)) 
 
 
 ROUND(x,n)  of  FIXED(p,q)  is no longer supported if n < (q - p) (when the rounding would be too far to the left) 
 In  ROUND(x,n) , if x is  FIXED(p,q)  and n < 0, then the result now has the attributes  FIXED(p-q+1,0) 
 
       

Language changes    Scale factors must be non-negative, hence:   divides that produces negative scale factors are no longer supported. 
 negative scale factors in declares of  FIXED  and in the precision-handling built-in functions are no longer supported.

Content: Migrating from earlier releases of  Enterprise PL/I  to  Enterprise PL/I   6.2 
   
 This  Migration Guide  concentrates on the migration effort in migrating from  OS PL/I  or  PL/I for MVS & VM  to  Enterprise PL/I   6.2 . If you have already moved to  Enterprise PL/I  3, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 5.1, 5.2, or 5.3, migration to  Enterprise PL/I   6.2  is relatively easy. 
 This chapter focuses on differences in the compiler options and in the compiler messages, but there are some other differences in the compiler that will affect users of earlier release of  Enterprise PL/I : 
   The compiler itself is compiled with ARCH(10) and any use of the compiler on a machine with older hardware could cause the compiler to abend. 
 Linking and executing of the code generated by the compiler must be done with LE 2.4 or later. 
 The compiler itself is now also a 64-bit application. This means the user exit defined by the IBMUEXIT module must also be a 64-bit module. If you are not using the default IBMUEXIT supplied by IBM as part of the compiler, then you must    declare all the POINTERs in the control blocks passed by the compiler to the exit as POINTER(32) 
 recompile your IBMUEXIT code with the LP(64) compiler option 
 bind it as a 64-bit module 
  The  Programming Guide   provides details on how to do this, but it is important to note that the bind step for 64-bit code is significantly different than the traditional bind step for 31-bit code. It is particularly important to note that if CEEV2Rx is the prefix for your LE 2.4 (or later) datasets, then   the binder parameters must include AMODE=64,DYNAM=DLL,RENT 
 
 SYSLIB must specify //SYSLIB   DD DSN=CEEV2Rx.SCEEBND2,DISP=SHR
 
 
 SYSLIN must include //         DD DSN=CEEV2Rx.SCEELIB(IBMPQV11),DISP=SHR
//         DD DSN=CEEV2Rx.SCEELIB(CELQS003),DISP=SHR 
 
 SYSIN must specify (instead of ENTRY IBMUEXIT) ENTRY CELQSTRT
Migrating from earlier releases of Enterprise PL/I to Enterprise PL/I 6.2
SYSLIN must include //         DD DSN=CEEV2Rx.SCEELIB(IBMPQV11),DISP=SHR
//         DD DSN=CEEV2Rx.SCEELIB(CELQS003),DISP=SHR 
 
 SYSIN must specify (instead of ENTRY IBMUEXIT) ENTRY CELQSTRT 
 
   
 The compiler no longer supports the NUMBER/NONUMBER option, but the STMT/NOSTMT option is still supported, and NOSTMT is still the default. If the STMT option is specified, then the listing will have the same format as under NOSTMT except that in certain parts of the listing there will be an additional column immediately to the right of the NUMBER column (which shows the source line and file numbers). This additional column will show the logical PL/I statement number, if any.

Changes in the OPTIMIZE compiler option    The  OPTIMIZE  compiler option has undergone these changes:   Compile times under  OPTIMIZE (0) will be (potentially significantly) slower than under previous versions. 
 Under 6.1,  OPTIMIZE (TIME) and  OPTIMIZE (2) both map to  OPTIMIZE (3). As such, comparisons of compile times under 6.1 and under previous releases are valid only if  OPTIMIZE (3) is used when compiling under a previous release.

Content: EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
Specifying an EBCDIC file encoding to use with the language servers    
 The language servers parse programs using the IBM-037 code page by default. If your program uses a different target encoding on z/OS, you must specify an EBCDIC code page for the language server to use, so it can compute the correct line length. This encoding should match the EBCDIC encoding used, when the file is placed back on z/OS. This functionality currently supports only the COBOL and PL/I language servers. 
 Here is how Z Open Editor evaluates what encoding to pass to the language server: 
 
 
 For local COBOL or PL/I programs, you must configure the  zopeneditor.encodings.filePatterns  settings object. 
 
 
 This setting maps file name glob patterns to an EBCDIC file encoding. These patterns is specified as glob patterns. A single asterisk  *  matches any number of characters within a path segment, including none. A double asterisk  **  matches any number of path segments, including none. For example,  { **/COBOL/*.cbl : IBM-930 }  assigns any file paths that contains a directory named  COBOL  ending with a  .cbl  extension an encoding of  IBM-930 . ([Learn more about how to specify glob patterns.](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns)) 
 
   
 
 For remote programs (accessed through Zowe Explorer), you can do any of the following: 
 
 
 If an RSE API profile is used to access the file (such as a data set opened in Zowe Explorer), Z Open Editor first looks for an encoding specified by your RSE mappings as documented  above  (either in a  rseapi  profile in your  zapp.yaml  or the location in the  zopeneditor.zowe.defaultRseConversionMappingsFile  setting). 
 
 
 If no RSE mappings exist or if you are using a z/OSMF profile to access the file, you can specify an encoding in the Zowe Explorer profile you are using to access the program (see the  encoding  property example in this  section ).
EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
You can use the  zopeneditor.encodings.filePatterns  user setting for remote files, but you must adjust the glob pattern to match to remote files in the Zowe Explorer filesystem (described  here ). 
 
   
   These settings only control what encodings are passed to the language servers. To control encodings used for file conversions when you upload or download z/OS resources, use an RSE API mappings file or  rseapi  ZAPP profile, or specify the  encoding  property in your Zowe profile. 
 When a program is opened that is associated with an encoding using one of the methods above, a counter titled "EBCDIC Byte Count" is visible in the Visual Studio Code status bar. This counter displays two numbers: the number of bytes in the line up of the cursor's current position (accounting for the source code page), and the maximum number of bytes enabled in the line (controlled by the  zopeneditor.language.maximumLineLength  setting). As with the previous functionality, this counter only displays for COBOL and PL/I programs. 
 If the language server detects double-byte characters, it displays guillemets (»«) at the position of the SOSI codes, when applicable. These guillemets are decorative and not stored with the program or affect its line length.
EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
Character conversion using .gitattributes    
 The  .gitattributes  file enables you to specify how files are encoded when it is checked out to the directory you work and when it is stored in the Git repository. This is particularly useful to handle double-byte characters. 
   How it works   
 
 
 User Build from VS Code: When you perform a user build on an existing COBOL file that contains double-byte characters, the  .gitattributes  settings ensure that the file is encoded in IBM-930 when it is checked out to the working directory. 
 
 
 Build process: During the build process, the file is uploaded to the specified USS folder with the correct encoding that is mentioned in the  .gitattributes . 
 
 
 File display in VS Code: When you open the file in VS Code, the double-byte characters are correctly converted from IBM-930 to UTF-8. 
 
     Example workflow   
 
 
 Update the  .gitattributes  file located at the root of the repository with the following line. This specifies an encoding of IBM-930 for all files in the repository with the  .cbl  file extension:  *.cbl zos-working-tree-encoding=ibm-930 git-encoding=utf-8 . 
 
 
 Perform a user build from VS Code on an existing COBOL file that contains double-byte characters using the right-click menu. 
 
 
 During the build process, the  zos-working-tree-encoding  parameter specifies the code page used to encode files that are uploaded to USS or MVS. 
 
 
 Wait for the build process to complete. Once finished, the COBOL file is uploaded to the specified USS folder using the encoding from  .gitattributes . 
 
 
 When opened in VS Code, the Japanese characters is correctly converted from IBM-930 to UTF-8. 
 
     Example file with double-byte characters   こんにちは、世界！ //* Hello world!
これはテストファイルです。 //* This is a test file.
IBM-930エンコーディングを使用しています。 //* Using IBM-930 encoding.
#

 ATTENTION:  Le courant du conducteur de protection peut dépasser 10 mA. Risque de choc électrique. Assurez-vous que la connexion à la terre est réalisée avant le raccordement à l'alimentation. (C053)       
 警告:  保护导体电流可能超过 10 毫安。存在电击风险。请确保在连接电源之前已接地。(C053)       
 注意:  保護導體電流可能超過 10 mA。存在電擊風險。在連接電源之前，請確保已接地。(C053)       
 Pozor:  Struja unutar zaštitnog vodiča može prelaziti 10 mA. Opasnost od električnog udara. Osigurajte da se napravi uzemljenje prije priključivanja na struju. (C053)       
 POZOR:  Proud ochranného vodiče může přesáhnout 10 mA. Nebezpečí úrazu elektrickým proudem. Před připojením zdroje zajistěte připojení k zemi. (C053)       
 Pas på:  Strømstyrken i beskyttende leder kan overstige 10 mA. Fare for elektrisk stød. Der skal etableres jordforbindelse, før der tilsluttes strøm. (C053)       
 Let op!:  De stroom op de beschermingsgeleider kan meer dan 10 mA bedragen. Risico op schok. Zorg ervoor dat de verbinding geaard is voordat de stroomtoevoer wordt aangesloten. (C053)       
 ETTEVAATUST:  Kaitsejuhi vool võib ületada 10 mA. Elektrilöögi oht. Enne toiteühenduse loomist veenduge, et tehtud on maandusühendus. (C053)

ETTEVAATUST:  Kaitsejuhi vool võib ületada 10 mA. Elektrilöögi oht. Enne toiteühenduse loomist veenduge, et tehtud on maandusühendus. (C053)       
 Varoitus:  Suojajohtimessa voi kulkea yli 10 mA:n virta. Sähköiskun vaara. Varmista maadoitus ennen virransyötön kytkentää. (C053)       
 Vorsicht:  Schutzleiterstrom überschreitet möglicherweise 10 Milliampere. Gefahr eines Stromschlags. Stellen Sie sicher, dass vor dem Anschluss der Stromversorgung eine Erdverbindung hergestellt wurde. (C053)       
 ΠΡΟΣΟΧΗ:  Το ρεύμα στους προστατευτικούς αγωγούς ενδέχεται να υπερβαίνει τα 10 mA. Κίνδυνος ηλεκτροπληξίας. Πριν από τη σύνδεση της τροφοδοσίας, βεβαιωθείτε ότι υπάρχει σύνδεση με τη γείωση. (C053)             
 FIGYELMEZTETÉS:  A védővezetőben folyó áram meghaladhatja a 10 mA-t. Áramütés veszélye. Gondoskodjék róla, hogy a földelés be legyen kötve a tápellátás csatlakoztatása előtt. (C053)       
 Avvertenza:  La corrente del conduttore di protezione può superare 10 mA. Rischio di scossa. Assicurarsi che sia effettuata la connessione alla messa a terra prima di alimentare la connessione. (C053)       
 注意:  保護伝導体が現在 10 mA を超えそうです。感電のリスク。電源に接続する前に、アースの接続をしっかり確認ください。(C053)       
 경고:  보호 도체 전류는 10mA를 초과할 수 있습니다. 충격의 위험이 있습니다. 전원에 연결하기 전에 반드시 접지하십시오. (C053)       
 UZMANĪBU:  Aizsargvada strāva var pārsniegt 10 mA. Pastāv trieciena risks. Pārliecinieties, vai ir nodrošināts zemējums pirms padeves savienojuma. (C053)       
 ПРЕДУПРЕДУВАЊЕ:  Струјата во заштитниот проводник може да надмине 10 mA. Постои ризик од струен удар. Уверете се дека е поврзано заземјување пред да поврзете извор на напојување. (C053)       
 
   
 Oprez:  Struja zaštitnog provodnika može biti veća od 10 mA. Rizik od šoka. Uvjerite se da postoji veza sa uzemljenjem prije povezivanja dovoda. (C053)       
 ADVARSEL:  Strøm i beskyttelsesleder kan overskride 10 mA. Fare for elektrisk støt. Sørg for at kobling til jord er gjort før kobling til strømtilførsel. (C053)

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/SS2RWS_3.2.0/com.ibm.zsecure.doc_3.2.0/carla_lang/carla_cmnd_lang_list_fam_cmds_unix_fl_type.html
Score: 0.2069793939590454
Content: File type     The following table list the possible file type values (FILETYPE format).  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     TYPE   file type   meaning   
       -   regular file   Contains data   
   b   block special file   For example, a disk or CD-rom (but this does not occur in USS)   
   c   character special file   For example, a tty or printer   
   d   directory   Contains files   
   e   external link   A UNIX name for  an MVS data set (on z/OS® only) or  a PDS(E) member   
   l   symbolic link   Contains another UNIX pathname to look up instead   
   p   pipe (or FIFO)   A FIFO communication stream between two programs   
   s   socket   A network connection   
       Note that 'hard link' is not a file type. In UNIX a file does not really have a name but is identified by an inode number. A file is primarily referred to via one or more path names (known as  hard links ) where that  inode  number appears in the directory.

[Rank 3] Title: z/OS Security responsibilities and considerations
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/zos/3.2.0?topic=systems-security-responsibilities-considerations
Score: 0.13917888700962067
Content: Security responsibilities and considerations     z/OS UNIX  maintains system security by verifying user identities and file access control information. A PFS is primarily concerned with file access control.   
 For those functions where POSIX .1 (IEEE Standard 1003.1-1990) specifies that  appropriate privilege  is required, the PFS refers to a bit that is set by the LFS to determine whether the function has appropriate privileges. For more information, see  Appropriate Privileges  in the POSIX standards. 
 Access control checks are based on information that is stored with each individual file, and are generally carried out on the system where the data resides. 
 Access control is integrated with the SAF interface to call RACF®, or whichever security product is used at a particular installation. 
 The basic flow of file security is as follows:    Security information, such as the owner's UID-GID and the permission bits for a file, is kept in a 64-byte area called the  file security packet  (FSP), which is mapped by IRRPIFSP.  The FSP is the security-related section of a file's attributes. 
 The FSP is created by a SAF call from the PFS when a file is created. Some of the information is taken from the current security environment, and some of it is passed as parameters. 
 The PFS stores the FSP with the attributes of the file. 
 When an access check is to be done, the PFS calls SAF with the type of check that is being requested, the audit_structure from the current call, and the file's FSP. SAF passes these to the security product, which extracts user information from the current security environment and compares it against the access control that is stored within the FSP. The audit_structure is used primarily for any auditing that may be necessary.  There are many access and privilege checks defined by the POSIX standards. The detailed description of each vnode operation in  PFS operations  discusses the access checks that are expected.
Security responsibilities and considerations
When a file's access control information is changed, such as by  chmod() , the PFS calls SAF with the type of change, the new values, the audit_structure from the current call, and the file's current FSP. A new version of the FSP is returned to the PFS, which then replaces the file's old FSP with the new one. 
 
 When a file is deleted, the PFS discards the FSP. 
     In the flow described previously, the PFS provides some private space within the file attributes for the security product's use, ensures common access checking across all PFSs, allows for the installation of different security products, and lets the security product perform auditing or other non-POSIX processing. 
 The PFS is ultimately responsible for the following access checks:    If the PFS controls the storage of its own files, it follows the flow outlined in this topic to create, maintain, and use security information. 
 If the PFS is a client getting its data from some remote repository, it sends the request to the remote system, where the access checks are performed using the osi_getcred service.  
 If access is not controlled for the type of data that is supported by a particular PFS, the PFS may choose to skip these security procedures. 
     Some events that occur in the LFS are audited for security purposes by the vn_audit operation. For example, because relative pathnames may be audited during an access check, it is important to audit the working directory so that a full path name can be constructed if necessary. When a user calls  chdir()  or  fchdir() , the LFS invokes vn_audit to record the new working directory.  chroot() , which changes the current root, is another call that causes an audit record to be created. 
 PFS support for multilevel security  discusses PFS responsibilities and considerations for multilevel security.
#


[Rank 4] Title: IBM Explorer for z/OS RSE as a Java application
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/explorer-for-zos/3.4.0?topic=explorer-rse-as-java-application
Score: 0.12073594331741333
Content: RSE as a Java application     Figure 1. RSE as a Java application       Figure 1  shows a basic view of resource usage (processes and storage) by RSE. 
 RSE is a Java™ application, which means that it is active in the z/OS® UNIX environment. This allows for easy porting to different host platforms and straightforward communication with the  z/OS Explorer  client, which is also a Java application (based on the Eclipse framework). Therefore, basic knowledge of how z/OS UNIX and Java work is very helpful when you try to understand  z/OS Explorer . 
 In z/OS UNIX, a program runs in a process, which is identified by a PID (Process ID). Each program is active in its own process, so invoking another program creates a new process. The process that started a process is referenced with a PPID (Parent PID), the new process is called a child process. The child process can run in the same address space or it can be spawned (created) in a new address space. A new process that runs in the same address space can be compared to executing a command in TSO, while the spawning one in a new address space is similar to submitting a batch job. 
 Note that a process can be single- or multi-threaded. In a multi-threaded application (such as RSE), the different threads compete for system resources as if they were separate address spaces (with less overhead). 
 Mapping this process information to the RSE sample in  Figure 1 , we get the following flow:    When the RSED task is started, it executes BPXBATSL, which invokes z/OS UNIX and creates a shell environment – PID 50331904. 
 In this process, the  rsed.sh  shell script is executed, which runs in a separate process (/bin/sh) – PID 67109114. 
 The shell script sets the environment variables and executes Java with the required parameters to start the RSE daemon – PID 50331949. 
 RSE daemon will spawn off a new shell in a child process (RSED8) – PID 307.
RSE as a Java application
RSE daemon will spawn off a new shell in a child process (RSED8) – PID 307. 
 In this shell, the environment variables are set and Java is executed with the required parameters to start the RSE thread pool – PID 308. 
     RSE is capabable of running in 31-bit or 64-bit addressing mode, resulting in different storage limits. In 31-bit mode, the available storage is limited to 2 GB, while in 64-bit mode, there is no limit, unless specified in SYS1.PARMLIB. 
 Java applications, such as RSE, do not allocate storage directly, but use Java memory management services. These services, like allocating storage, freeing storage, and garbage collection, work within the limits of the Java heap. The minimum and maximum size of the heap is defined during Java startup. When running in 64-bit mode, Java will attempt to allocate the heap above the 2 GB bar, freeing up space below the bar. 
 This implies that getting the most out of the available address space size is a balancing act of defining a large heap size while leaving enough room for z/OS to store a variable amount of system control blocks (dependent on the number of active threads).
#

Content: file - Determine file type     

Format    file  [ -BcdEh ] [ -f   filelist ] [ -M   magic ] [ -m   magic ] [ -W   option [, option ] …]   file ...  file  ... 
 file   -i  [ -h ] [ -f   filelist ]  file  ... file  ...
file - Determine file type
Description    file  determines the format of each  file  by inspecting the attributes and (for a regular file) reading the contents of the  file . If the  file  is an executable, its addressing mode is determined for output. If  file  is not an executable,  file  compares each  file  to entries found in one or more  magic  files to determine their file type. If you specify - as a file name,  file  reads from the standard input (stdin).  
 file  then divides files that do not match a template in the  magic  file into text files and binary  data. Then, by reading the text files and making an informed guess based on the contents,  file  further divides text files into various types such as C programs, assembler programs, files of commands to the shell, and  yacc  or  lex  programs. 
 
 file  displays the name of each file along with the file type.    If the variable _UNIX03=YES is set, a space is used to separate the file name and the type.  
 If the variable _UNIX03 is unset or is not set to YES, a tab is used to separate the file name and the file type. 
     The  file  utility uses three types of tests to determine the file type: the file attribute tests, the position-sensitive tests and the context-sensitive tests.    The file attribute tests determine file types such as directory, character special, FIFO, socket, symbolic link, and external link. 
 The position-sensitive tests determine file types by looking for certain string or binary values at specific offsets in the file being examined. The default position-sensitive tests are defined by:     The  /etc/magic  file 
 The AMODE test built into the  file   utility 
  If a magic file test succeeds, the message field of the line will be printed and no further tests will be applied, except for tests on immediately following lines beginning with a single > character.

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=programming-ztpf-support-mongodb

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB   
 
 With  z/TPF support for MongoDB , remote distributed platforms can access and update data in a  z/TPF  database by using the  MongoDB Query Language .   You do not need to change  z/TPF  application code to use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .   MongoDB  is a NoSQL database and treats data as documents.  MongoDB  documents are described by using   JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) , which is an open and human- and machine-readable standard to facilitate data exchange. The  z/TPF  database is not a NoSQL database, but you can create a  JSON  document from the data in the  z/TPF  database. 
       
 Access z/TPF data by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  The  z/TPF   Internet Daemon  ( InetD ) is used to access the  z/TPF  data by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  z/TPF support for MongoDB  is provided only for  z/TPFDF  databases.  
 
 MongoDB terminology  Some concepts in  z/TPFDF  and  MongoDB  are similar, but the terms to refer to these concepts might be different. 
 
 z/TPFDF database definition (DBDEF) considerations   z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports only R-type  z/TPFDF  files. Some settings in the  z/TPFDF  database definitions change the behavior of  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Add default keys by using z/TPFDF default key support  With  z/TPFDF default key support for z/TPF support for MongoDB , you can define default keys for  z/TPFDF  files in the  z/TPFDF collection descriptors  ( adbi.xml  files). 
 
 Setting up z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must define a  z/TPF  server for  MongoDB  before you can connect  MongoDB  remote clients to the  z/TPF system  by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .
z/TPF support for MongoDB
Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB security  To maintain a secure environment, you must implement controls to ensure that users have access only to data that they are authorized to access.  
 
 z/TPF user security   By using  z/TPF user security , you can define  z/TPF  user IDs, passwords, and privileges to  z/TPF  data and resources. You can use  z/TPF user security  only for   z/TPF support for MongoDB  applications.  
 
 Analyze the performance of z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can use   resource usage by owner name collection  on the  z/TPF system  to collect resource usage information for the  MongoDB  applications based on the owner name. You can specify the high-level qualifier and mid-level qualifier in the  resource usage by owner name configuration file  to collect resource usage information by specific categories.  
 
 Operations and coverage considerations for z/TPF support for MongoDB  There are operational considerations to remember when you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 User exits for MongoDB request processing  For each  MongoDB  request,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  provides two user exits, the pre-request user exit (UMON_pre_request) and post-request user exit (UMON_post_request) for you to control pre-request and post-request processing.  
 
 Filter collections by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  A filtered collection is a logical subset or view of a collection or a subset of logical records (LRECs) of a  z/TPFDF  file. As a database administrator, you can use filtered collections to control the visibility of the data in a collection.

Content: z/TPFDF  database definition (DBDEF) considerations   
 z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports only R-type  z/TPFDF  files. Some settings in the  z/TPFDF  database definitions change the behavior of  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 Specifying the following parameters on the DBDEF macro have effects on  z/TPF support for MongoDB : 
   Default key parameters   If a  z/TPFDF  file is not defined with default keys, an error is produced when you try to update a document in the collection that represents the  z/TPFDF  file by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  You can query documents that do not have organization defined in the  z/TPFDF  database definitions. When a  z/TPFDF  file contains LRECs that have different logical records IDs and the file is not organized by logical record ID, the behavior of a  MongoDB  query for that file is unpredictable. 
 To avoid updating the DBDEF macros of existing databases, you can define default keys for  z/TPFDF  files in  z/TPFDF collection descriptors  by using the  z/TPFDF default key support for z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 AUTODEINDEX   If you specified  AUTODEINDEX=YES  in the database definition for a  z/TPFDF  file, the document is  automatically deindexed when the document is deleted by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . If all records are removed from the document, the document is automatically deindexed and the document is deleted.  If you specify  AUTODEINDEX=NO  in the database definition for a  z/TPFDF  file, you must deindex the document from all of the indexed paths before you delete a document or define automatic indexing rules for each index path so that  z/TPF support for MongoDB  can perform the deindexing for the application.
z/TPFDF database definition (DBDEF) considerations
Note:  Custom indexes in the  z/TPFDF collection descriptor  are not deindexed even if you specified  AUTODEINDEX=YES . You must deindex any custom indexes before you delete the document or define automatic indexing rules for each defined custom index so that  z/TPF support for MongoDB  can perform the deindexing for the application.   
 KEYCHECK   If you specified  KEYCHECK=YES   in the database definition for a  z/TPFDF  file, an update request through  z/TPF support for MongoDB  to change the organization of a record is rejected.  
 SEQUPDT   If you specified  SEQUPDT=YES   in the database definition for a  z/TPFDF  file, the sequence update counter is returned when a  MongoDB   remote client requests a document in the  z/TPFDF  file.  To ensure consistency, you can request conditional updates based on whether the sequence update number of the document matches the value that is passed by the  MongoDB   remote client. If the sequence update number does not match the value that is passed by the  MongoDB   remote client,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  indicates that the document was not found and you must retrieve the document again. For more information, see the  update()  method. 
 
 UNIQUE   If you specified  UNIQUE=YES   in the database definition for a  z/TPFDF  file, uniqueness is verified when records are inserted or updated in a document by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . If you try to insert a record into a document and a record already exists with matching organization, an error is returned to the remote client.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB  ( APARs  PJ42292 and PI33010)   
 z/TPF support for MongoDB   provides the ability to access  z/TPFDF  databases from remote distributed systems by using the standard  MongoDB  query language without requiring changes to z/TPF applications.  
 Previously, to request access to the  z/TPF  data on the  z/TPF system  from a remote distributed system, custom applications were required on the  z/TPF system  and the remote distributed systems that access the  z/TPF  data. The custom  z/TPF  applications required accessing the  z/TPF  databases and formatting  z/TPF  binary data for the remote distributed system applications. Implementing the custom applications on the  z/TPF system  might have the following results:   The implementation of the custom interfaces was time consuming.  
 
 z/TPF  application programmers and remote application developers were involved to maintain custom interfaces.  
 Different custom interfaces might need to be developed and deployed, because remote distributed systems might require different formats and functionality.  
     With  z/TPF support for MongoDB , remote distributed systems can access the  z/TPFDF  databases by using the standard  MongoDB  clients. Standard  MongoDB  clients exist in different programming languages, and you can install standard  MongoDB  clients on different remote distributed platforms.  
 z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports many  MongoDB  programming services. With these  MongoDB  programming services, you can get information or access documents in the  z/TPFDF  databases.  
 Accessing  z/TPFDF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB  does not require any changes to the  z/TPF  applications. However, to use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , the code must be built with the  GCC  4.6 ( version tpf-11r1-13 or later ) or the Dignus Systems/C or Systems/C++ V1.98 (version 1.98.68 or later) compiler.  
 For more information about  APARs   PJ42292  and PI33010, see the APEDITs.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB  data definition considerations   
 When you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , the  DFDL schema file  describes the contents of the  z/TPFDF  file. The  DFDL schema file  for the  z/TPFDF  file defines the field names and data types for the  z/TPFDF  binary data.  
       
 Supported data types and representations  The  MongoDB  query language supports all  DFDL  data types and representations that are supported on the  z/TPF system  except for the date, time, and dataTime data types.  
 
 Special data type considerations  You can convert the fields that  z/TPF support for MongoDB  treats as strings to any data type that the  MongoDB  remote client can use. 
 
 Update z/TPFDF logical records that contain variable length fields   z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports fields that are defined as variable length in the  DFDL schema file  that describes a  z/TPFDF  file.  
 
 Update fields that are represented as an array of elements   z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports fields that are represented as an array of elements in the  DFDL schema file  that describes a  z/TPFDF  file.  
 
 Update control fields in z/TPFDF logical records  A  DFDL  control field is a field that changes the overall layout of the  z/TPFDF  logical record (LREC).  
 
 Represent choice statements in z/TPF support for MongoDB  When a  z/TPFDF  logical record (LREC) contains a choice statement, but the choice statement does not contain a discriminator to define the choice value,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  uses the first choice path that was defined when a document for this logical record is built. 
 
 Add padding, trimming, and encoding attributes  For strings that are defined in the  DFDL schema file  that describes a  z/TPFDF  file, you can optionally modify the padding, trimming, and encoding attributes.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB  programming   
 This information describes the  MongoDB  programming methodology that is used to interface with  z/TPF  data. 
 Examples that are provided in this information are one of the following types:   Programmatic examples that use the  MongoDB  Java™ client driver . 
 Shell based examples that describe the actual input document. You can use standard shell-based tools to send requests from a graphical user interface (GUI) or command line.  
           
 Connect to z/TPF support for MongoDB on the z/TPF system   
 
 Access the z/TPF database by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  When the  MongoDB  remote client connects to the  z/TPF system  and the  MongoDB  remote client is authenticated, the  MongoDB  remote client can access the  z/TPF  database.  
 
 Retrieve collections by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can retrieve individual collections from the  z/TPF  database after  MongoDB  remote clients access the database, for example, a  z/TPFDF  file that is named PNR.  
 
 Understand the ObjectId value in z/TPF support for MongoDB  In standard  MongoDB , documents that are saved in a collection require a unique ID field to be associated with the document. The ObjectId value is the representation of this unique identifier. In the  z/TPF system , the ObjectId value represents the file address of the prime block of the  z/TPFDF  subfile, which is unique for every subfile in a  z/TPFDF  file. The ObjectId value, in the  z/TPF system , is a 12-byte value that consists of an 8-byte hexadecimal file address that is right justified. 
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB data definition considerations  When you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , the  DFDL schema file  describes the contents of the  z/TPFDF  file. The  DFDL schema file  for the  z/TPFDF  file defines the field names and data types for the  z/TPFDF  binary data.
z/TPF support for MongoDB programming
Use automatic indexing rules for z/TPF support for MongoDB  With standard  MongoDB  servers, you can add indexes for fields in the document that allows optimized retrieval when the document is located by using that field. The indexes for these fields are maintained by the standard  MongoDB  server. Maintenance of these indexes is transparent to the end user who accesses the standard  MongoDB  server. 
 
 Retrieve documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can retrieve the documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you get a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Insert documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can insert documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Update documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can update documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Remove documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can remove documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Logging for z/TPF support for MongoDB  With logging for  z/TPF support for MongoDB , you can log  MongoDB  requests and responses and send the logging data to a server in binary JSON (BSON) format.  
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB error messages  When you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , certain situations might   cause the  z/TPF   MongoDB  server to return  an error. For example,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  returns an error to the  MongoDB  client when a user tries to update a document but does not have authority to update.

Content: z/TPFAR  support     The  z/TPF application requester (z/TPFAR)  is middleware that provides a method of accessing  z/TPF  applications to read and write data directly to any remote database server that is compliant with Distributed Relational Architecture (DRDA). For example, you can use  z/TPFAR  with a  z/TPF  application to directly access and update data residing on a remote IBM®  Db2®  subsystem. You also can use  z/TPFAR  to move  Db2  data to  z/TPF  applications. Structured Query Language (SQL) provides an interface between DRDA-compliant database servers and a  z/TPF  application. When you use  z/TPFAR , SQL commands are included in a  z/TPF  application program that is coded in assembler, C, or C++ language. 
 You can use  z/TPFAR  to enhance your enterprise in the following processing areas:    Transaction logging, which transfers data between the  z/TPF system  and a remote system.  Use transaction logging when data resides on the  z/TPF system , but the decision support is done on the remote application server. 
 
 Bulk data transfer, which sends large amounts of data to a remote system.  Use bulk data transfer when the data resides on the  z/TPF system , but the decision support is done on the remote application server, which can contain data with a high number of changes that is not current with the  z/TPF  data. Bulk data transfer also is useful when only certain pieces of the data are needed on the remote  Db2  subsystem. 
 
 Single line query, which retrieves a single data record from the remote system.  Use the single line query when there are a relatively low number of  z/TPF  transaction requests for data that normally resides on the remote application server. 
 
 Block query, which retrieves multiple data records from the remote system.  Use the block query with data that resides on the remote application server and a refresh of that data is needed on a  z/TPF system .

[Rank 2] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition Other z/TPF system storage requirements
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=requirements-other-ztpf-system-storage
Score: 0.22486788034439087
Content: Other  z/TPF system  storage requirements     z/TPF application requester  affects storage on the  z/TPF  base system. When an SQL call is issued, all processing for that ECB is suspended until control is returned. 
 
 Note:  When developing an application, be careful of any locks, file records, or core blocks associated with an ECB over an SQL call. All processing for this ECB is suspended until a response is received from the remote AS.  This can result in a  z/TPF system  resource problem.   For  z/TPFAR , you need to assess the following  z/TPF system  resources to ensure that storage requirements are adequately met:     
 Heap storage :  z/TPFAR  uses the malloc function for all of its storage requirements. The exact amount of heap storage needed by  z/TPFAR  is dependent on the type of SQL requests made by the  z/TPF system  applications. For instance, an SQL INSERT command with many host variables defined as characters will take up more storage than an SQL INSERT command with two host variables defined as short integers. 
 
 #IBMMP4 records : Ten IBM® miscellaneous processor-unique records (#IBMMP4) are defined for the SQL database management system directory (SDD). 
 
 TPF/APPC  fastpath :  TPF/APPC  uses OM (output message) records to queue messages received. In most  z/TPF system s, most OM records are not VFA candidates.  A separate record ID X'FF0F' is used to queue messages for conversations with  z/TPFAR ; the new record type is a VFA candidate.  Copying data from VFA instead of doing I/Os improves performance. 
 
 Short term pools : Short term pools are used to store the SQL transaction profile (STP) and associated blocks when the DBSAC and DBSDC macros/functions are used.  The DBSDC macro/function detaches the associated blocks from the ECB and files them out in short term pools.
Other z/TPF system storage requirements
Attention:  Ensure that the short term pool cycle time is large enough for records to still be present when the DBSAC macro/function is used to reattach the STP and associated blocks.   See  z/TPFAR working storage blocks  for more information about the DBSAC and DBSDC macros/functions.  See also   z/TPF General Services  and   z/TPF C/C++ Language Support User's Guide  for additional information about the DBSAC and DBSDC macros/functions.

Content: Application requester   
 
 The  z/TPF application requester (z/TPFAR)  supports IBM's Distributed Relational Database Architecture (DRDA) strategy for database distribution using the remote unit of work method of distributed access. DRDA is a relational database connection architecture, consisting of protocols for communications between an application and a remote database, and for communications between databases.  Distributed access involves working with data that is located on remote systems. A relational database is a database in which the data is organized and accessed according to relations. Structured Query Language (SQL) is a programming language used to define relational data, access relational data, and control access to relational data resources.   z/TPFAR  permits you to share data between any DRDA- compliant database servers, such as a  Db2®  relational database and a  z/TPF  application using the SQL interface. The component of  Db2  that allows the  z/TPFAR  connection is known as an application server (AS). For more information about the concept of an application server, see  Access to remote data  or the  Distributed Relational Database Architecture Reference . An LU 6.2 conversation or a  TCP/IP  connection is used to connect a  Db2  subsystem with  z/TPFAR . By using  z/TPFAR , a  z/TPF  application can directly access and update the information residing on the remote  Db2  subsystem.

 Figure 1  shows the basic flow of an application transformed from source code to object code on a  z/TPF system , and the bind process, which converts DBRM output from a  Db2®  precompiler to a usable control structure known as a  bind file . The bind process performs a complete error check and access strategy for each SQL command. In C, C++, or assembler programs, you can run the bind process directly on  Db2  offline (static binding) before you run the application. In  C language , the  z/TPF system  can perform a bind at run time (run-time binding).  Figure 1.  z/TPF  application preparation overview         z/TPF  application programs must be precompiled using the  Db2  precompiler on a z/OS® or Linux® system.  Application programming  The  z/TPFDF product  provides an interface between application programs that request access to information in a database and the system software that physically accesses the stored data. 
 
 C language functions  The  z/TPFDF  C language functions are set up in groups. All the functions in any one group perform a similar service.

[Rank 3] Title: CICS Transaction Server for z/OS EXEC CICS ENQ
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/cics-ts/6.x?topic=summary-enq
Score: 0.07456091791391373
Content: EXEC CICS ENQ
Options  
   LENGTH( data-value )    specifies as a halfword binary value the length of the resource to be enqueued on. The value must be in the range 1 through 255; otherwise, the LENGERR condition occurs. If the LENGTH option is specified in an ENQ command, it must also be specified in the DEQ command for that resource, and the values of these options must be the same. You must specify LENGTH when using the method that specifies a data value containing a unique argument, but not for the method that specifies a data area as the resource. It is the presence or absence of LENGTH that tells CICS which method you are using. 
 MAXLIFETIME( cvda )    specifies the duration of the ENQ to be automatically released by CICS. CVDA values are:     UOW    The duration of the ENQ is a unit of work. Examples are a syncpoint rollback or syncpoint, if the application does not issue a DEQ before the unit of work ends. This is the default value.   
 Note:  For compatibility, a CVDA value of LUW is also supported.   
 TASK    The duration of the ENQ is a task. The enqueue carries over the units of work within the task. Use MAXLIFETIME(TASK) with great care because other tasks issuing ENQ commands on the same resource could be suspended until the end of this task. 
   There are two ways to code this option.     You can assign a CVDA value with the translator routine DFHVALUE. This allows you to change a CVDA value in the program. For example:     MOVE DFHVALUE(UOW) TO AREA-A
EXEC CICS ENQ RESOURCE(RESNAME)
              MAXLIFETIME(AREA-A)     
 If the required action is always the same, you can declare the value directly. For example:     EXEC CICS ENQ RESOURCE(RESNAME) UOW     or     EXEC CICS ENQ RESOURCE(RESNAME) TASK
EXEC CICS ENQ
If the required action is always the same, you can declare the value directly. For example:     EXEC CICS ENQ RESOURCE(RESNAME) UOW     or     EXEC CICS ENQ RESOURCE(RESNAME) TASK     
     
 NOSUSPEND    specifies that the application program is not to be suspended if the resource on the ENQ command is unavailable, but the ENQBUSY condition occurs.   Note, however, that if a HANDLE CONDITION for ENQBUSY is active when the command is executed, action, control is passed to the user label supplied in the HANDLE CONDITION. This takes precedence over the NOSUSPEND option but is, of course, negated by either NOHANDLE or RESP.  
 
 RESOURCE( data-area )    identifies the resource to be enqueued on by:     Specifying an area whose address represents the resource. 
 Specifying a variable that contains the resource (an employee name, for example). In this case, you must use the LENGTH option.
EXEC CICS ENQ
Conditions  
   55 ENQBUSY    occurs when an ENQ command specifies a resource that is unavailable and the NOSUSPEND option is specified, or there is an active HANDLE CONDITION ENQBUSY.   If the NOSUSPEND option is not specified, and the ENQ command specifies a resource that is unavailable, the application program is suspended and the ENQBUSY condition is not raised. 
 Default action: ignore the condition. 
 
 16 INVREQ    RESP2 values: CVDA values are:     2   The MAXLIFETIME option is set with an incorrect CVDA. 
   Default action: terminate the task abnormally. 
 
 22 LENGERR    RESP2 values:     1   The value specified for the LENGTH option is outside the range 1 through 255. 
   Default action: terminate the task abnormally. 
 
     
 

Examples  
 Two tasks, enqueuing on the same resource and specifying a data area that is the resource, must refer to the same location in storage. They could both, for example, refer to the same location in the CWA.     EXEC CICS ENQ
     RESOURCE(RESNAME)       Two tasks, enqueuing on the same resource and specifying a data area that contains a unique argument, can refer to the same location or to different locations, but the contents of the locations must be the same. The length must be supplied in the LENGTH option.     EXEC CICS ENQ
     RESOURCE(SOCSECNO)
     LENGTH(9)       The two methods cannot be combined. If one task uses the LENGTH option, and the other task does not, CICS regards the enqueues with and without the LENGTH option as different types of enqueues, and the tasks are not serialized.

Content: Deallocate
2   Deallocate_confirm   Specifies to execute the function of the Confirm service and if it is successful, deallocate the conversation normally.   
 Note:  You cannot specify Deallocate_confirm for a conversation with a synchronization level of syncpt.     
 3   Deallocate_abend   Specifies to run the function of the Flush service and deallocate the conversation abnormally. Do not invoke deallocate_abend following a Post_on_Receipt. Transaction programs that issue Deallocate_abend after Post_on_Receipt might not regain control after issuing the deallocate. 
 
     
 Notify_type   Supplied parameter     Type:  Structure 
 Char Set:  N/A 
 Length:  4-8 bytes 
   Specifies the type of processing and notification (synchronous or asynchronous) requested for this service. Programs can request asynchronous processing, which returns control to the program immediately and later notifies the program by ECB when the service is complete.  The possible types are:     None   No notification is requested.  The service is performed synchronously, and control is returned to the caller when processing is complete.  All returned parameters are set on return to the caller. To specify no notification, set the parameter value to a four-byte structure containing binary zeros. 
 
 ECB   Programs can request asynchronous processing by specifying an ECB to be posted when processing completes. To specify an ECB, set the parameter to an eight-byte structure containing a fullword binary one (X'00000001') followed by the address of a fullword area to be used as the ECB.  The ECB must reside in the home address space.
Deallocate
When you specify an ECB, control is returned before processing is complete, with only the return code set.  If the asynchronous request was accepted, the return code is set to 0 to indicate that the service is being processed asynchronously.  Other returned parameters are filled in during asynchronous processing, and the specified ECB is posted when all returned parameters are set.  The completion code field in the ECB contains the return code for the service. 
 
     
 Return_code   Returned parameter     Type:  Integer 
 Char Set:  N/A 
 Length:  32 bits 
   Return_code specifies the return code that is returned to the local program.  In cases where an error code is returned, the program should not examine any other returned variable associated with the call as nothing is placed in the variables. 
 See the next section for descriptions of return codes that can be returned to a caller of Deallocate.

The CI/CD pipeline is based on Git for source code management (SCM), while IBM® Dependency Based Build (DBB) and zAppbuild are required for the Build component. For the remaining components of the CI/CD pipeline, enterprises will generally select one technology for each component category, although sometimes more than one IDE option is selected (depending on developer preference). 
 
 Note:   We have listed common options for each CI/CD component below. However, if you do not see the option your enterprise has selected for a particular component, that does not necessarily mean it cannot align with our guidance. For most tools being used elsewhere, you can integrate them into the pipeline as long as they are compatible with z/OS application development and bring value to your enterprise.   Not sure what tool to pick for certain CI/CD component? See our documentation on   How do you select what tool to use for each component .

Integrated development environment      Who needs to install the integrated development environment (IDE), and where? 
   The integrated development environment (IDE) will need to be installed by z/OS application developers on their local workstations or be included in the enterprise software distribution process. IBM supports the following IDE options for z/OS application development:      IBM Developer for z/OS   
   IBM Developer for z/OS on VS Code   
   
 Some IDE options have host components that require a system programmer to configure. 
       IBM Developer for z/OS     IBM's Eclipse-based IDE [IBM Developer for z/OS (IDz)](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/developer-for-zos) needs to be installed on the local workstations of the z/OS application developers. 
 IDz also contains various z/OS host components that need to be installed by the system programmer. Please refer to the [host install and configuration section](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/developer-for-zos/latest?topic=installing-configuring-host-components) in the IDz documentation or use the interactive [host configuration assistant](https://zdev-hca.ibm.com/). This generic benefit can be broken down into the following, and will be discussed in more detail: Improving productivity Improving application quality Improving database integrity Controlling recoup using applications. First, several different abstract data representations are provided, and for each representation, many predefined data manipulation routines are available. Together, all of these routines form a standardized C (C++) library of APIs. As a result, time is not needed on designing new data models and corresponding functions from the beginning. This allows an application to be completed much faster than it would be otherwise. Code is reused over and over, saving time and money. Second, application quality can be greatly improved by using the z/TPFCS library. It is less likely that problems will be found with code that has been used several times before than if new code was written. Furthermore, z/TPFCS APIs hide the low-level z/TPF interfaces, including ECB usage, data event control block (DECB) usage, and file address information. Because less z/TPF -specific skills are needed, education time and costs are also reduced. Next, using z/TPFCS can improve database integrity. With different collection types and corresponding data manipulation operations available, you are able to find an abstract representation that best matches your data and use a set of consistent APIs with that data. Furthermore, by using this support, it is possible for z/TPFCS database users to access and retrieve information from the collection without having to retrieve the entire collection. Benefits of z/TPFCS In addition, z/TPFCS provides several different locking mechanisms for concurrency control to ensure that the database remains in a consistent state at all times. Furthermore, utilities are available for database maintenance and testing. This includes utilities to examine data, repair data that may be corrupted, and capture and restore data. Finally, z/TPFCS enables applications to control how data is recouped instead of requiring recoup descriptors to be set up in advance. Content: One application and a simplistic network     In the 1960s, the  z/TPF system  was designed for the airline reservation application, the only application in a  z/TPF system . Therefore, by default, all terminals in a network attached to a  z/TPF  processing facility were  logged onto  the only application (the airline reservation application). Also, at that time, the technology of terminal networks was rather simplistic, with communication controllers providing little more function than line multiplexing. As such, the  z/TPF system  (also called a host system) was responsible for:    Requesting input from the terminal interchanges in the network, also called polling.  In a network where communication controllers provide only minimal function, the host system (the  z/TPF system  in this case) must check whether data has been input from terminals. Contrast this with a modern communication controller that performs this function on behalf of the host to which it is attached. 
 
 Scheduling output (that is, responses) to those same terminals.  In a network where communication controllers provide only minimal function, if a device is not ready to receive data, the data (that is, a response) must be queued by the host system (that is, the  z/TPF system ) until the device is ready to receive it. Compare this to a modern communication controller that takes the data from the host and buffers it until the device is ready to receive it. 
 
     An application program addressed terminals by physical addresses. The  z/TPF system  handled the unique interfaces that were required for each different device type (similar to a communication protocol). The application recognized a terminal by its terminal address in the form of line number (LN), interchange address (IA), and terminal address (TA) or LNIATA.
#

Content: tpf_mount: Mount a  file system  to the  z/TPF system 
   
 This function grafts a file system object onto the file system tree at a point you specify. The contents of the file system become available through the new mount point directory. Any files in the directory at the time of a successful mount become invisible and are unavailable until the file system is detached, unless otherwise specified by the  MNT_UNION  parameter.

tpf_mount: Mount a file system to the z/TPF system
Last updated      Changed for  PUT15 . 
 Changed for  PUT04 . 
 Added for  PUT00 . 
     

Format    #include <sys/imount.h>
int tpf_mount(int type, const char *dir, int flags, void *data); 
         type   The type of file system that you want to mount. For a list of the file system types, see the  sys/imount.h  header file. 
 dir   A pointer to the path name of the directory on which the file system is to be mounted. 
 flags   Option flags. The following flags are valid for this parameter:    MNT_FORCE   Forces a file system from read write to read only. 
 MNT_RDONLY   The file system is read only; even the superuser can not write to it. 
 MNT_NOEXEC   Specifies that files cannot be executed from the file system. 
 MNT_NOATIME   Disables file access time updating. 
 MNT_NODEV   Specifies that special device files will not be interpreted on the file system. 
 MNT_NOSYMFOLLOW   Indicates to not follow symbolic links that are found on the file system. 
 MNT_UNION   Allows the files in the directory designated by  dir  to be visible after the file system is mounted. You will be able to search or read files from  dir , but any files created will be created in the file system that is mounted on  dir  unless it is mounted as a read-only file system. 
 MNT_UPDATE   Indicates that the  tpf_mount  function is being applied to a file system that is already mounted. This allows you to change the mount flags without requiring that you detach and mount the file system again. Some file systems are not allowed to be updated. For example, the  z/TPF collection support file system (TFS)  does not support a change from read-write to read-only.  If you specify MNT_UPDATE without specifying MNT_RDONLY, a read-only file system will be upgraded to read-write. 
   
 data   A pointer to a structure that contains the file system-specific arguments for the  tpf_mount  function. The format for these argument structures is file system specific.
#

Content: Use the  z/TPF mail service 
   
 You can use the  z/TPF mail service  to send an email from an application with the  tpf_mail  function. 
 The  z/TPF mail service  uses  guaranteed delivery for JVM  to send the email request with a guarantee that delivery is tried at least once. To use this service, you must use an  SMTP server  that is external to the  z/TPF system . 
 The following figure illustrates the email message flow with the  z/TPF mail service .  Figure 1. Email message flow with the  z/TPF mail service         The parameters from the  tpf_mail  function are used to create an email request that is sent to a local MQ input queue, such as TPFMAIL.INPUT.QUEUE, which is defined for the  z/TPF mail service . 
  If the email request is successfully placed on the local MQ input queue, the  tpf_mail  function returns TPF_MAIL_SUCCESS. If the email request is not successfully placed on the local MQ input queue, the  tpf_mail  function returns TPF_MAIL_FAILURE. If the request fails, the email request is not sent to the tpfmail JAM for further processing. The details of the failure are displayed in an online error message, and the email delivery is not tried. 
 When the email request is successfully placed on the local MQ input queue, the request is sent to the tpfmail JAM for processing. 
 The  z/TPF mail service  tries to connect to an  SMTP server  that is external to the  z/TPF system . The connection parameters are specified in a mail service properties file. If the connection is successful, the email is sent to the  SMTP server  for delivery. If the connection is unsuccessful, an error message is logged in the  stderr.log  file if log4j is configured. 
 When a response from the  SMTP server  indicates that the email was accepted for delivery, this is considered a guaranteed delivery. If the email was not accepted for delivery, an error message is logged in the  stderr.log  if log4j is configured, and the email is discarded.
Use the z/TPF mail service
Configuring the z/TPF mail service  You must configure the  z/TPF mail service  for your system before you can send email requests from applications with the  tpf_mail  function. 
 
 z/TPF mail service properties files  You must create a mail service properties file that specifies the connection properties for an  SMTP server  that is external to the  z/TPF system .
#

 The application page of  IBM® watsonx Code Assistant for Z Code Optimization Advice  consists of the Application overview tab, Programs tab, Problems tab, and the Environment details section. This page shows all information at the application level.
Application page
Application overview tab    The Application overview is the first view that displays. It shows the performance of the application, timing statistics, programs that are top candidates for optimization, CPU allocation, a summary of runtime options, and environment details. Use this view to determine where to start optimizing program performance. 
 Timing statistics 
 This chart shows key performance metrics about the application being analyzed, including:   CPU time: The amount of time the processor spends executing instructions. This is the most stable and reliable metric for evaluating the performance of COBOL code. CPU time does not include time spent on I/O operations, waiting for processing resources, user input, or responses from subsystems or other facilities. 
 Elapsed time: The total wall-clock time measured from the start to the end of an application's run. It includes both active processing time and wait times for I/O, resource availability, and subsystem responses. Comparing elapsed time to CPU time helps determine if an application is CPU-bound. A significantly larger elapsed time suggests the application spends more time outside of COBOL code execution. 
 Total Problem CPU Impact: Shows the percentage of processing time spent on instructions flagged as performance issues. A higher value means the program spends more time in code that could be optimized.  
 Note:  This is only an indicator, not a guarantee of improvement, fixing all problems may not reduce CPU usage by the exact percentage shown.   
 Application samples: Samples are the primary metric used to measure and calculate CPU time and percentage. A sample represents an instance when the profiler observes the execution of an instruction in the application’s compiled code. Each time the profiler observes the execution of an instruction, the number of samples attributed to that instruction increases by one.
