[Rank 4] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition REST consumer message flow
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=support-rest-consumer-message-flow
Score: 0.10055699199438095
Content: REST  consumer message flow   
 The  z/TPF system  builds a  REST  service request that is sent by a  z/TPF  application, transforms the response into a single response structure and passes back the response to the application. 
 The following procedure describes the  REST  consumer message flow:   An application calls the  tpf_srvcInvoke  or  tpf_srvcInvoke_ext  function and passes the following information:   The name of the service 
 The request data 
 The place to store the response data 
   
 The  z/TPF system  locates the  z/TPF service descriptor  by using  common deployment  for the name of the service or the operation ID. If the  z/TPF service descriptor  is not found or not deployed, a status code of 503 is returned. 
 The  z/TPF system  locates the  OpenAPI descriptor  by using  common deployment  for the name of the service or the operation ID. If the  OpenAPI descriptor  is not found or not deployed, a status code of 404 is returned. 
 The request data is transformed into an HTTP request by using the  DFDL  parser with the URL and method that are created from what is provided for the corresponding operation ID in the  OpenAPI descriptor . 
 If a value other than  localhost  is specified for the host field in the  OpenAPI descriptor , the  z/TPF  HTTP client is used to call the  REST  service. Otherwise, the service provider that the providerType element specifies in the  z/TPF service descriptor  is used to route the request to a local service provider. For example, if the providerType element is set to JAM, a  z/TPF  Java™ application is used to implement the service. 
 The response is sent to the  z/TPF  HTTP client synchronously or asynchronously, or to the  z/TPF system  in the case of a local service provider. 
 The  z/TPF system  locates the  OpenAPI descriptor  and the  z/TPF service descriptor  that was used for the request by using the operation ID.
REST consumer message flow
The  z/TPF system  locates the  OpenAPI descriptor  and the  z/TPF service descriptor  that was used for the request by using the operation ID. 
 The HTTP response is serialized into a response structure and response data by using the  DFDL  parser. 
 The response is returned to the application or the asynchronous program. 
     Figure 1. HTTP client REST consumer message flow

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=rest-provider-support
Score: 0.0868753120303154
Content: REST provider support   
 REST provider support  uses the  z/TPF HTTP server  to implement a  REST  service provider by creating an  OpenAPI descriptor  to describe the  REST  service and a  z/TPF service descriptor  to describe the  z/TPF  implementation details for that service. 
 A  REST  service requester begins a conversation by sending an HTTP message. The HTTP message arrives at the  z/TPF system  over the network. The  z/TPF system  processes the HTTP message and creates a response, which is returned to the  REST  service requester over the network. By configuring the  OpenAPI descriptor  and the  z/TPF service descriptor , the HTTP request and response format is completely hidden from the service wrapper program that you create to call a  z/TPF  application to process the  REST  service. 
       
 REST provider message flow  The  z/TPF HTTP server  receives a  REST  request and responds to the client that sent the  REST  request. 
 
 Using REST provider support  You can use  REST provider support  to process  REST  service requests.
#

[Rank 1] Title: IBM Developer for z/OS The Wazi Deploy packager command
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/developer-for-zos/17.0.x?topic=commands-wazi-deploy-packager-command
Score: 0.2112402468919754
Content: The  Wazi Deploy  packager command   
 The  Wazi Deploy  packager creates a build in the artifact repository to upload the content of a local folder that contains the artifacts of an application, or creates a local package file in a specified working folder. It also produces the application manifest file that will be used by the  Wazi Deploy  generation command.  
   This local folder is not created by  Wazi Deploy . It is typically a z/OS UNIX System Services partition in a z/OS environment or a standard folder in a distributed environment. The structure of the local folder is free. It can have folders and files. The files must have an explicit extension, which will be used as the type that you define in the deployment method.  Wazi Deploy  does not provide any facility to create the content of this folder. 
 To start the packager, enter a  wazideploy-package  UNIX command line.  
   
 The following code shows the syntax of the command.   
   usage: wazideploy-package [-h] [-mn manifestName] [-mv manifestVersion] [-md manifestDescription] [-m manifest] [-me manifestExtension] [-meo manifestExtensionOptions]
                          [-bn buildName] [-bN buildNumber] [-bu buildUrl] [-lf localFolder] [-cf configFile] [-r repository] [-rp repositoryPath] [-ut {archive,folder}]

Content: The  Wazi Deploy  packager command   
 The  Wazi Deploy  packager creates a build in the artifact repository to upload the content of a local folder that contains the artifacts of an application. It also produces the application manifest file that will be used by the  Wazi Deploy  generation command.  
   This local folder is not created by  Wazi Deploy . It is typically a z/OS® UNIX System Services partition in a z/OS environment or a standard folder in a distributed environment. The structure of the local folder is free. It can have folders and files. The files must have an explicit extension, which will be used as the type that you define in the deployment method.  Wazi Deploy  does not provide any facility to create the content of this folder.

Content: EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
Specifying an EBCDIC file encoding to use with the language servers    
 The language servers parse programs using the IBM-037 code page by default. If your program uses a different target encoding on z/OS, you must specify an EBCDIC code page for the language server to use, so it can compute the correct line length. This encoding should match the EBCDIC encoding used, when the file is placed back on z/OS. This functionality currently supports only the COBOL and PL/I language servers. 
 Here is how Z Open Editor evaluates what encoding to pass to the language server: 
 
 
 For local COBOL or PL/I programs, you must configure the  zopeneditor.encodings.filePatterns  settings object. 
 
 
 This setting maps file name glob patterns to an EBCDIC file encoding. These patterns is specified as glob patterns. A single asterisk  *  matches any number of characters within a path segment, including none. A double asterisk  **  matches any number of path segments, including none. For example,  { **/COBOL/*.cbl : IBM-930 }  assigns any file paths that contains a directory named  COBOL  ending with a  .cbl  extension an encoding of  IBM-930 . ([Learn more about how to specify glob patterns.](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/glob-patterns)) 
 
   
 
 For remote programs (accessed through Zowe Explorer), you can do any of the following: 
 
 
 If an RSE API profile is used to access the file (such as a data set opened in Zowe Explorer), Z Open Editor first looks for an encoding specified by your RSE mappings as documented  above  (either in a  rseapi  profile in your  zapp.yaml  or the location in the  zopeneditor.zowe.defaultRseConversionMappingsFile  setting). 
 
 
 If no RSE mappings exist or if you are using a z/OSMF profile to access the file, you can specify an encoding in the Zowe Explorer profile you are using to access the program (see the  encoding  property example in this  section ).
EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
You can use the  zopeneditor.encodings.filePatterns  user setting for remote files, but you must adjust the glob pattern to match to remote files in the Zowe Explorer filesystem (described  here ). 
 
   
   These settings only control what encodings are passed to the language servers. To control encodings used for file conversions when you upload or download z/OS resources, use an RSE API mappings file or  rseapi  ZAPP profile, or specify the  encoding  property in your Zowe profile. 
 When a program is opened that is associated with an encoding using one of the methods above, a counter titled "EBCDIC Byte Count" is visible in the Visual Studio Code status bar. This counter displays two numbers: the number of bytes in the line up of the cursor's current position (accounting for the source code page), and the maximum number of bytes enabled in the line (controlled by the  zopeneditor.language.maximumLineLength  setting). As with the previous functionality, this counter only displays for COBOL and PL/I programs. 
 If the language server detects double-byte characters, it displays guillemets (»«) at the position of the SOSI codes, when applicable. These guillemets are decorative and not stored with the program or affect its line length.
EBCDIC code pages and mappings files
Character conversion using .gitattributes    
 The  .gitattributes  file enables you to specify how files are encoded when it is checked out to the directory you work and when it is stored in the Git repository. This is particularly useful to handle double-byte characters. 
   How it works   
 
 
 User Build from VS Code: When you perform a user build on an existing COBOL file that contains double-byte characters, the  .gitattributes  settings ensure that the file is encoded in IBM-930 when it is checked out to the working directory. 
 
 
 Build process: During the build process, the file is uploaded to the specified USS folder with the correct encoding that is mentioned in the  .gitattributes . 
 
 
 File display in VS Code: When you open the file in VS Code, the double-byte characters are correctly converted from IBM-930 to UTF-8. 
 
     Example workflow   
 
 
 Update the  .gitattributes  file located at the root of the repository with the following line. This specifies an encoding of IBM-930 for all files in the repository with the  .cbl  file extension:  *.cbl zos-working-tree-encoding=ibm-930 git-encoding=utf-8 . 
 
 
 Perform a user build from VS Code on an existing COBOL file that contains double-byte characters using the right-click menu. 
 
 
 During the build process, the  zos-working-tree-encoding  parameter specifies the code page used to encode files that are uploaded to USS or MVS. 
 
 
 Wait for the build process to complete. Once finished, the COBOL file is uploaded to the specified USS folder using the encoding from  .gitattributes . 
 
 
 When opened in VS Code, the Japanese characters is correctly converted from IBM-930 to UTF-8. 
 
     Example file with double-byte characters   こんにちは、世界！ //* Hello world!
これはテストファイルです。 //* This is a test file.
IBM-930エンコーディングを使用しています。 //* Using IBM-930 encoding.

 Figure 1  shows the relative position of the  z/TPFDF product  in a  z/TPF system .   Figure 1.  z/TPFDF  application programs in  z/TPF         The  z/TPF system  must be in 1052 state or above before  z/TPFDF  applications can be run. If the application requires  z/TPFDF  files that use pools,  get file storage  ( GFS ) must be active before the  z/TPFDF  application is started.

Content: Installing and customizing the  z/TPFDF product 
     The  z/TPFDF product  is a  database  manager for application programs that run in a  z/TPF  operating environment. To increase the productivity of application programmers, the  z/TPFDF product  provides:    A logical method to organize the  database 
 
 A set of standardized assembler macros or C functions that form the  application programming interface  ( API ) 
 Central routines to access and manage the  database 
 
 Utilities for  database  maintenance and testing. 
     After you install the  z/TPFDF product ,  z/TPFDF  application programs are no longer sensitive to the physical implementation of the  database . Installation and use of the  z/TPFDF product  is separate from the  z/TPF system , but the  z/TPFDF product  is built by using the same makefile-based build process.

[Rank 4] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition z/TPF file system support
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=ds-ztpf-file-system-support
Score: 0.11916474252939224
Content: z/TPF file system support     The  z/TPF system  supports the following  file system s:     z/TPF collection support file system (TFS) 
 Memory file system (MFS) 
 Fixed file system (FFS) 
 Pool file system (PFS) 
 Process pseudo-file system (PROCFS) 
 
 System pseudo-file system (SYSFS) . 
 
 Version control file index (VCFX) . 
     
 Figure 1  shows the  virtual file system (VFS)  and the  file system s that the  z/TPF system  supports. Figure 1.  z/TPF   file system s     File ownership and accessibility in the  file system  are controlled by using the  POSIX -compliant structures of user ID, group ID, and access permissions associated with each file in the  file system . Application programs can interact with the  file system  through  file system  C functions. 
 You also can use the following commands to manage the  file system :    The ZAVFS and ZDVFS commands allow you to change and display  file system  configuration and trace information. 
 The ZFILE commands are a set of commands that allow you to work with and manage files on the  file system . 
 The ZOVFS and ZPVFS commands provide  file system security  and allow you to control who can work with files on the  file system . 
 The ZFILE pax and ZFILE tar commands allow you to archive and restore files from one  z/TPF system  to another and between a UNIX or  Linux®  system and a  z/TPF system . 
     To use  z/TPF file system support , you must initialize the  z/TPF collection support file system (TFS) ; see  Initializing the z/TPF collection support file system  for more information. If the TFS is already initialized, but you need to increase the number of file system records, or if you need to increase the size of the  PFS  or the  FFS , see  Increasing the number of file system records .
z/TPF file system support
Manage file system mount points  The  z/TPF system  uses a number of directories as mount points for the file system. For some of these directories, you must mount a  specific file system on that directory to enable a particular z/TPF capability. Additionally, for some mount points, you can mount a file system other than the  z/TPF collection support file system (TFS)  and gain certain efficiencies. 
 
 Initializing the z/TPF collection support file system   
 
 Increasing the number of file system records   
 
 Building a fixed file system  Use this procedure to create a  fixed file system (FFS) . 
 
 Building a pool file system  Use this procedure to create a  pool file system (PFS) . 
 
 Process pseudo-file system and system pseudo-file system support   
 
 Initializing the version control file index  Initialize the  version control file index (VCFX)  so that the  VCFX  can be referenced through the  /sys/tpf_pbfiles  symbolic link in the  system pseudo-file system (SYSFS) . 
 
 File system security support   
 
 Managing file system state files  If the current working directory or environment variables for  ZFILE  commands are changed, a state file is created for the terminal that issues these  ZFILE  commands.  
 
 TFS directory backup support  You can use the backup collection attribute to back up a directory in the  z/TPF collection support file system (TFS) .  
 
 ZFILE fsck problem report for the TFS  The  ZFILE fsck  problem report lists problems that are generated when you use the  ZFILE fsck  command in the  z/TPF collection support file system (TFS) . You can use the report to analyze and repair the problems. 
 
 File system conventions  You can use various coding and system administration conventions when you work with file systems on the  z/TPF system  to address security, data integrity, file system health, and performance.

Content: DBB public repositories   The DBB public repositories in Git provide sample DBB scripts and snippets that you can use, instead of writing your own build scripts with the DBB APIs. The following DBB public repositories are available: 
   The [DBB Community Repository](https://github.com/IBM/dbb) provides samples that you can use to write simple build scripts or pipeline stages with the DBB APIs. For example, you can deploy build outputs to artifact repositories. The              HelloWord  sample provides simple source file types and the Groovy build scripts to compile them. 
 The [DBB zAppBuild Repository](https://github.com/IBM/dbb-zappbuild) provides a complete build application sample that you can use to build z/OS® applications with Apache Groovy build scripts and IBM Dependency Based Build (DBB) APIs.             The  Mortgage  application is provided among these samples to quickly test the build process. 
 The [DBB-Git Migration Modeler](https://github.com/IBM/dbb-git-migration-modeler) helps with scoping the applications boundaries and migrating z/OS applications to Git by using DBB.
#

Content: Using the PPF Operand     You can use the PPF operand to install, migrate, build, and delete a specific copy of a single product. Before you can use the PPF operand, however, you must have a usable form product parameter file for the copy of the product you are installing, migrating, building, or deleting. The usable form product parameter file is a product parameter file after all overrides have been applied and variables have been resolved. The usable form product parameter file can be:     Shipped with the product by IBM 
 Created manually using the VMFPPF EXEC 
     The usable form product parameter file contains the product installation parameters for one copy of the product. A usable form product parameter file also has a unique name, which you may assign, to identify the specific product installation parameters for this copy of the product. In the VMFINS command syntax, this unique name is referred to as the  ppfname . 
 As an example, to install a product using the PPF operand, you can enter: 
 vmfins install ppf  ppfname  ( options 
 The format is the same for build, migrate, and delete. For examples of how to use the PPF operand, see  Scenario 1: Installing a Product with the PPF Operand ,  Scenario 1: Building a Product with the PPF Operand , and  Scenario 1: Deleting a Product with the PPF Operand .

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/systems-hardware/linuxone/3932-AGL?topic=object-fulfill-ficon-storage-volume
Score: 0.08945059776306152
Content: Fulfill FICON Storage Volume   
 The  Fulfill FICON Storage Volume  operation maps the ECKD storage resource that has been configured by a SAN administrator to a storage volume that is part of a request for new or modified FICON® storage. 
 

HTTP method and URI    POST /api/storage-groups/ {storage-group-id} /storage-volumes/ {storage-volume-id} /operations/
   fulfill-ficon-storage-volume   In this request, the URI variable  {storage-group-id}  is the object ID of the Storage Group object and the URI variable  {storage-volume-id}  is the element ID of the storage volume element. 
   

Request body contents    
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     Field name   Type   Rqd/Opt   Description   
       control-unit-uri   String/ URI   Required   The canonical URI of the storage control unit in which the backing ECKD volume is defined.   
   unit-address   String (2)   Required   A two-character lower case hexadecimal number that represents the unit address of the backing ECKD volume within the storage control unit.
Fulfill FICON Storage Volume
Description    This operation provides information about the ECKD storage resource that has been selected by a SAN administrator to fulfill a base storage volume that is part of a request for new or modified FICON storage. Until this information is provided, the CPC does not have all the data it needs to address and connect to that storage resource. 
 Once a FICON storage volume has been fulfilled, the storage control unit and unit that has been assigned to it cannot be changed. If the  size ,  cylinders  or  model  properties of a volume are modified, the  fulfillment-state  of the volume is changed to  "pending" , indicating that action may be necessary by the storage administrator to adjust the size of the backing ECKD volume. The  fulfillment-state  of the volume is changed back to  "complete"  by fulfilling the volume again with the exact same  control-unit-uri  and  unit-address , indicating that the changes have been completed. 
 If the API user does not have action/task permission to the  Configure Storage – Storage Administrator  task, a 403 (Forbidden) status code is returned. A 404 (Not Found) status code is returned if the object ID  {storage-group-id}  does not identify a storage group object to which the API user has object-access permission, or the element ID  {storage-volume-id}  does not identify a storage volume in the storage group,  or the  control-unit-uri  in the request body does not identify a storage control unit,  or the current value of the group’s  type  property is not  "fc" .

The following code fragment shows how to use  IMSQueueConnectionFactory   to obtain and use a  QueueConnection  object.     
  IMSQueueConnectionFactory jmsConnectionFactory = new IMSQueueConnectionFactory();  QueueConnection jmsConnection = null;  QueueSession jmsQueueSession = null;  Queue jmsQueue = null;  QueueRequestor jmsQueueRequestor = null;           try {      jmsConnectionFactory.setTimeout(1000);    //Set 10 second timeout      jmsConnectionFactory.setResponseAreaLength(128000);    //Allocate 128K response area      jmsConnection = jmsConnectionFactory.createQueueConnection();      jmsQueueSession = jmsConnection.createQueueSession(false, Session.AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE);      jmsQueue = jmsQueueSession.createQueue("OTMDEST1");                  jmsQueueRequestor = new QueueRequestor(jmsQueueSession, jmsQueue);      TextMessage sendMsg = jmsQueueSession.createTextMessage();                  String msg = "My Message";      sendMsg.setText(msg);      TextMessage replyMsg = (TextMessage)jmsQueueRequestor.request(sendMsg);      System.out.println("Received message: "+replyMsg.getText());  } catch (Exception e) {      e.printStackTrace();  }

Content: Java command line to run  OMEGAMON Data Connect 
   
 Whichever platform you choose, you can use a Java™ command line to run  OMEGAMON® Data Connect . 
 

Before you enter the Java command line    In the shell where you will enter the Java command line, perform the following actions: 
   If you choose to run  OMEGAMON Data Connect  on z/OS®, deactivate automatic code page conversion of tagged files. For example, set the z/OS UNIX environment variable  _BPXK_AUTOCVT  to  OFF . Reason for this action: on z/OS, automatic code page conversion can cause the Java virtual machine to misinterpret  OMEGAMON Data Connect  configuration files. 
 
 Change the current working directory to the  OMEGAMON Data Connect  user directory that you want to use for this instance of  OMEGAMON Data Connect . Reason for this action:  OMEGAMON Data Connect  treats the current working directory as the  OMEGAMON Data Connect  user directory.
Java command line to run OMEGAMON Data Connect
Example Java command line    java \
  -Xms1024m -Xmx4096m -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \         1  
  -Dfile.encoding=ISO8859-1 \                               2  
  -Djava.net.preferIPv6Addresses=system \                   3  
  -Dodp.ext= <odp_extensions_paths_list>  \                   4  
  -jar  <odp_installation_directory> /lib/odp-server.jar \    5  
  --spring.config.name=connect                              6       1    The initial heap size ( -Xms ) and maximum heap size ( -Xmx ) shown here are examples only. The maximum heap size must be large enough to accommodate the  OMEGAMON Data Connect    queue capacity  of each output. In practice, the default queue capacity meets typical requirements and fits within this example maximum heap size. 
 For more information on setting the heap size, see the advice on [how to do heap sizing](https://www.ibm.com/docs/SSA3RN_17.0/com.ibm.java.vm.17.doc/docs/mm_heapsizing.html) in the  IBM® Semeru Runtime® Certified Edition for  z/OS  documentation. 
 
  2    Setting the file encoding option avoids a potentially inappropriate system default encoding, such as EBCDIC on z/OS. 
  3    Setting the Java system property  java.net.preferIPv6Addresses  to  system  causes  OMEGAMON Data Connect  to resolve hostnames into IP addresses according to the order of IP addresses that the operating system returns for a hostname. That order determines whether  OMEGAMON Data Connect  uses an IPv4 address or an IPv6 address. For example, if you specify the hostname  myserver.example.com  as the value of an  OMEGAMON Data Connect  configuration parameter, then, if the operating system returns an IPv6 address before an IPv4 address for that hostname,  OMEGAMON Data Connect  uses the IPv6 address. 
 For more information about the order of IP addresses returned by the operating system and how to change that order, see the operating system documentation for the IP resolver.

Content: Navigating around the database
C Display block/CI    Enter  C  to display the contents of the current control interval or database block. The  Block/CI data  panel is displayed. 
   
   
 Tips:     After you make a selection, a message might be displayed. The message partly obscures the panel. To see the panel without the message, press PF8 and then PF7. Depending on the type of message, pressing Enter might refresh the panel. 
 Each time that you navigate to another segment in the database, an entry is made in the audit history file. You can view this file by selecting option  4. View audit history of processed segments  from the  Main menu . 
     IMS Database Repair Facility  follows these conventions when it evaluates entries on the  Segment Prefix  panel. 
   If navigate option F or B is specified, and a PTF, PTB, or PCF is selected, error message FABZ002W is displayed indicating that a conflicting selection was made. 
 If navigate option U, display option P (segment prefix), D (segment data), or C (Control Interval) is specified, and a PTF, PTB, or PCF is selected, the following error message is displayed:  FABZ002W: CONFLICTING SELECTION. SELECTED FIELDS WERE:
NAVIGATE OPTION, POINTER TYPE 
 
 If a PTF, PTB, or PCF with a zero RBA is selected, the following error message is displayed:  FABZ001W: END OF  xxx  POINTER CHAIN HAS BEEN REACHED. 
 
 If you select a PTF with a zero RBA in an HDAM database, the following error message is displayed:  FABZ047W: END OF SYNONYM (PTF) POINTER CHAIN HAS BEEN REACHED.

IMS Database Repair Facility  supports two methods for navigating through the database. One method is to use navigate options (Forward (F), Backward (B), and Up (U) options). [Rank 1] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition Dispense FARF6 pool file addresses
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=work-dispense-farf6-pool-file-addresses
Score: 0.15933647751808167
Content: Dispense  FARF6  pool file addresses   
 You can use the DBDEF macro to dispense  FARF6  pool addresses in a new or migrated database. 
 You can dispense  FARF6  pool addresses in the following ways:   Use the  F6PRP  or  F6OFP  parameter and optionally the  F6SHORT  parameter of the DBDEF macro to indicate that the  z/TPFDF product  must dispense  FARF6  pool addresses in a migrated database. 
 Use the  LD6  or  SS6  value on the  PF x  parameters of the DBDEF macro to indicate that the  z/TPFDF product  must dispense  FARF6  pool addresses in a new (nonmigrated) database. 
     If either of these indicators is set, one of the following conditions occurs:   If the  FARF6  migration switch is turned on, the  z/TPFDF product  uses the appropriate  FARF6  prototype record ID to dispense an actual  FARF6  pool address. 
 If the  FARF6  migration switch is not turned on, the  z/TPFDF product  uses the appropriate FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 prototype record ID to dispense a non- FARF6  pool address. 
     During  FARF6  migration, the  z/TPFDF product  determines the format of a new block based on the following rules that are used to determine the file address format:     If the  FARF6  migration switch is not turned on, FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 pool file addresses are dispensed regardless of any other rules. 
 If this block is an overflow block, file address format is determined as follows:    Because all blocks in a subfile must have the same file address header format, the file address header format that is assigned to the overflow block is the same as the file address header format that is used by the prime block. The  F6HDR  parameter of the DBDEF macro is ignored. 
 If the prime block uses an 8-byte file address header, you can use the  F6OFP  parameter of the DBDEF macro to determine the file address format for long-term addresses and use the  F6SHORT  and  F6OFP  parameters to determine the file address format for short-term addresses.
Dispense FARF6 pool file addresses
If the prime block uses a 4-byte file address header, the  F6OFP  parameter is ignored, and a FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 pool address is dispensed. A subfile can have both FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 and  FARF6  file addresses. 
   
 If this block is a prime block, you can use the  F6HDR  parameter of the DBDEF macro to determine the file address header format. In addition, you can use the  F6PRP  parameter to determine the file address format for long-term addresses and use the  F6SHORT  and  F6PRP  parameters to determine the file address format for short-term addresses. 
 To determine the file address format for index references when creating a new index LREC, the  z/TPFDF product  uses the  F6MIGIDX  parameter of the DBDEF macro for the index file and the  F6MIG  parameter for the detail file. A subfile can have both 4-byte and 8-byte file address references. 
 When restoring a file captured with the  CRUISE  utility, the  z/TPFDF product  will restore the file by using the file header and file address formats that were used when the file was backed up. The current DBDEF  FARF6  settings will be ignored. 
 When using the  DBTRD  and  DBTLD  commands to restore a file that is written to tape with the DBTLG macro (or equivalent C functions), the  z/TPFDF product  will use the file DBDEF settings at the time the file is restored to determine the file format. The DBDEF settings at the time of the restore must be compatible with the format of the data captured. For example, if the index LREC DBDEF settings when the file is restored do not match the format of the captured index LRECs, the results cannot be predicted.

Content: FARF6  support for  z/TPFDF 
   
 With  FARF6  support, you can use  FARF6  file addresses with the  z/TPFDF product . 
 You can use  FARF6  support under the following conditions:    You are running out of file addresses with your current applications. 
 Your planned expansion will cause you to require file addresses beyond the capabilities of FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5, and you want to reduce your migration effort by converting before the number of applications and databases grow. 
           
 Overview of FARF6 support for the z/TPFDF product   FARF6  support extends the number of file addresses that are available with the  z/TPFDF product  from 4 billion FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 file addresses to 72 quadrillion file addresses for all the fixed and pool file addresses.  FARF6  provides this extended range of file addresses by expanding 4-byte FARF3, FARF4, or FARF5 file addresses to 8-byte file addresses. 
 
 Options for migrating databases to use FARF6 pool file addresses  You can migrate your existing databases to use  FARF6  pool file addresses in stages. 
 
 Prepare the z/TPFDF product and applications for FARF6  You must prepare the  z/TPFDF product  and applications before you can use  FARF6  file addresses with the  z/TPFDF product . 
 
 How does FARF6 work?   
 
 Migrating to FARF6 file addresses   
 
 Summary of DBDEF macro FARF6 parameters   
 
 Updates to macros and C/C++ functions for FARF6   
 
 Updates to SW00SR for 8-byte file addresses  SW00SR file address fields are updated for 8-byte file addresses to support  FARF6 .

URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=mpif-mode0009i

Content: MODE 0009 I   IN STAGE FARF currmigstg , DISPENSING MODE IS FARF currmode  FARF6 ADDRESSING IS  status  TO THE SYSTEM FARF6 IS  dfstatus  FOR USE BY TPFDF FILES 
     

Where      currmigstg   The current FARF migration stage; for example, 3/4 or 4/5. 
 currmode   The current dispensing mode. 
 status   The status of FARF6 addressing for the  z/TPF system : either AVAILABLE or NOT AVAILABLE. 
 dfstatus   The status of FARF6 addressing for use by  z/TPFDF  files: either AVAILABLE or NOT AVAILABLE. 
     

Explanation  
 This is the normal response to the  ZMODE  command. This message displays the  file address reference format (FARF)  migration stage that is currently active and the FARF dispensing mode. In the FARF3 migration stage, dispensing is either in FARF3 or FARF4 formatted addresses. In the FARF4 migration stage, dispensing is either in FARF4 or FARF5 formatted addresses. An indication that FARF6 addressing is available to the  z/TPF system  means that the  z/TPF system  is ready to support FARF6 8-byte file addresses. This does not mean that FARF6 addresses are being used. An indication that FARF6 addressing is available for use by  z/TPFDF  files means that  z/TPFDF  databases can contain FARF6 file addresses. This does not mean that FARF6 addresses are being used. 
   

System action  
 None. 
   

User response  
 No action is required. 
   

Related information    See  z/TPF Operations  for more information about the  ZMODE  command.

Content: Installing and enabling  FARF6  on  z/TPFDF 
     Complete the following steps to install and enable FARF6:     Take one or all of the following actions:   Define one or more  FARF6  fixed record types. 
 Allocate  FARF6  pools as described in the  z/TPF Database User's Guide .

Content: MODE 0007 E   FARF6 ADDRESSING IS ALREADY ACTIVE ON THIS PROCESSOR 
     

Explanation  
 The  ZMODE  command was entered to activate FARF6 addressing, but FARF6 addressing is already active. 
   

System action  
 The command is rejected. 
   

User response  
 No action is required. 
   

Related information    See  z/TPF Operations  for more information about the  ZMODE  command.
#

Thought: I have retrieved relevant documents and no further retrieval is required for this user query.
Answer: 既存のデータベースをFARF6プールに移行するには、以下の手順を実行します。  
1. DBDEF マクロを使用して、FARF6 プール アドレスを新規または移行済みのデータベースに配布します。  
   - F6PRP または F6OFP パラメータ、およびオプションで F6SHORT パラメータを使用して、z/TPFDF 製品が移行済みのデータベースで FARF6 プール アドレスを配布するよう指示します。  
   - LD6 または SS6 値を DBDEF マクロの PF x パラメータに使用して、新規（非移行）データベースで z/TPFDF 製品が FARF6 プール アドレスを配布するよう指示します。  
2. z/TPFDF 製品が適切な FARF6 プロトタイプ レコード ID を使用して実際の FARF6 プール アドレスを配布するか、FARF6 移行スイッチがオフの場合は FARF3、FARF4、または FARF5 プロトタイプ レコード ID を使用して非 FARF6 プール アドレスを配布します。  
3. ZMODE T コマンドを入力して、FARF6 サポートを有効にします。  
4. z/TPFDF ロギング ファイル IR0VDF を初期化します。  
   - ZAREC LIDFU4.5 0 FDE60000C3E5C2C3  
   - ZAREC LIDFU4.5 8 0000000000000000  
   - ZAREC LIDFU4.5 10 001A00... (続きはドキュメントを参照)  

これにより、既存のデータベースが FARF6 プールに移行されます。

If the system does not prompt the operator, the system uses the values specified in LOADxx. If the SYSCAT and SYSPARM statements are not specified in LOADxx, the system issues one or both prompts to obtain the missing information. 
     Prompting for the Name of the Master Catalog:  If you choose an IMSI character that tells the system not to prompt for the master catalog name, the system uses the name specified on the SYSCAT parameter in the LOADxx parmlib member. 
 The default for the system parameter prompt is to use IEASYS00 in SYS1.PARMLIB, and the default for the master catalog prompt is to use SYSCATLG in SYS1.NUCLEUS. 
 The following table shows the possible values for the IMSI character. The default value is  period  (.).   
 
 Table 1. Possible values for IMS characters 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     IMSI character   Display informational messages   Prompt for master catalog response   Prompt for system parameters Response   
       
 period (.)  or  blank 
   No   No   No   
   A   Yes   Yes   Yes   
   C   No   Yes   No   
   D   Yes   Yes   No   
   M   Yes   No   No   
   P   No   Yes   Yes   
   S   No   No   Yes   
   T   Yes   No   Yes   
         
 The last character (character 8 of the LOAD parameter) specifies the      alternate nucleus identifier (0-9). Use this character at the system programmer's direction. If you do not specify an alternate nucleus identifier, the system loads the standard (or primary) nucleus (IEANUC01)  and an architectural extension of the nucleus (IEANUC11 or IEANUC21),  unless the NUCLEUS statement is specified in the LOADxx member. For more information, see [z/OS MVS Initialization and Tuning Reference](https://www.ibm.com/docs/SSLTBW_3.2.0/com.ibm.zos.v3r2.ieae200/abstract.htm).
Explanation of the A=INITIALIZE SYSTEM CONTROL PROGRAM, A2 Field
Also consider the following:   Decide whether to accept the system prompt indicator default. The default causes the system to suppress messages and not prompt the operator. You might miss critical messages during initialization, so you should review the hardcopy log.  New installations might want to select prompt feature A (display all messages and prompt the operator) or M (display all messages but do not prompt operator) on the Hardware Management Console while validating changes and analyzing system errors during the initialization process. Specifying either A or M might increase message traffic. 
 
 Omit the LOAD parameter when you accept all the IBM-supplied defaults. 
 Each character in the LOAD parameter is positional. If you change any of the defaults you must retype the characters or use periods (....) to hold the positions. 
 You cannot leave any leading spaces blank, unless the defaults are accepted for the rest of the LOAD parameter.

Content: System error processing     Errors may occur at any point of processing. There may be programming errors, such as incorrect function parameters, hardware malfunctions, and a variety of unusual conditions such as identification check failures on file operations. Three levels of errors are:     Hardware malfunctions that are overcome by retrying the I/O operation. In this case, error statistics are recorded, but the entry is insulated from the problem (for example, unit checks). 
 An error is detected by the from which the programs related to an entry may be able to recover. In this case the ECB-controlled program regains control. 
 An error is detected by the  z/TPF system  or the hardware from which the entry cannot recover (for example, an addressing exception generated by an ECB-controlled program). In this case the entry is forced to exit. 
 An error is detected that makes any more processing inadvisable. This is called  catastrophic failure  (for example, an operation exception in the  z/TPF system ). Such a failure is detected by various components of  z/TPF system  and may require a system restart. 
     The general philosophy of  z/TPF system  error processing is:     Save as much information as possible for the technical staff’s analysis and action. The amount of data saved is dependent on the severity of the error and its nature, whether program error or data integrity, for example. 
 Notify the central site that the error occurred. A message to the CRAS terminal will identify the error by number and the program in control at the time of the error. All system errors are documented in   z/TPF Messages (System Error, Offline, and Program Status Word) , which describe the cause of the error, the action taken by the  z/TPF system , and in some cases suggests actions to be taken by the application program or operations staff. 
 Respond to the program in control at the time of the error, if possible. 
 Determine if more processing may continue.
System error processing
Respond to the program in control at the time of the error, if possible. 
 Determine if more processing may continue. 
     If an ECB-controlled program is given control after an error is detected, then error indicators are set in the affected ECB. The program is assumed to contain the procedures to respond accordingly. These procedures typically include:     Providing a  selective  main storage dump of data pertinent to the active ECB 
 Sending an error message to the CRAS terminal 
 Either regaining control or forcing an exit of the ECB. 
     An important reason for returning control to the application (when possible) is to allow response to online terminal operators. The application can respond to the operator in the most meaningful manner once the condition is analyzed. If the  z/TPF system  is unable to return to the application program, it will force a standard message to be sent to the operator/terminal:   Check data and call supervisor . 
 Given the many possible errors and variations in the nature and complexity of applications, it is not meaningful to generalize about what the application should do. Designers and applications programmers must be alert to the possibility of errors at any point, and diligent in making the best possible response based on what is known. Additional information about  z/TPF system  error processing can be found in   z/TPF General Services  and   z/TPF System Services . Error processing with the control program save area in the ECB is discussed briefly in  Control program save area .

Content: Error recovery     Errors can occur at any point during  z/TPF  operations. There can be programming errors, such as incorrect macro parameters, or hardware malfunctions, or a variety of unusual conditions. The levels of error are:     Hardware malfunctions that are overcome by retrying the I/O operation.  In this case, error statistics are recorded but the Entry is protected from the problem (for example, unit checks). 
 An error detected by the system from which the programs related to an Entry may be able to recover.  In this case, the ECB-controlled program regains control (for example, a record identification check). 
 An error detected by the system from which the Entry cannot recover. In this case, the Entry is forced to exit (for example, an addressing exception generated by an ECB-controlled program). 
 An error detected by the system that makes continued operation of the system inadvisable. This is called a catastrophic error; for example, an operation exception (programming error) within the control program. Such a failure is detected and handled by various components of the control program and may require a system restart. 
     The basic objectives for   z/TPF system  error processing are:     Save as much information as possible for the technical staff's analysis and action 
 Notify the central site that the error has occurred 
 Respond to the program in control at the time of the error, if possible 
 Determine if operation of the system should continue.   If operation of the system is to continue, it must be restarted as quickly as possible.

[Rank 1] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition ROUTE_SETUP process
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=sessions-route-setup-process
Score: 0.12224707752466202
Content: ROUTE_SETUP process     When an RTP connection starts, there is a new flow called a ROUTE_SETUP command that occurs after the APPN search (LOCATE flows) and before the BIND request is sent out.  The purpose of the ROUTE_SETUP process is to gather the HPR information for the route, including:     The list of ANR labels in the forward direction (the path from the node containing the PLU to the remote RTP endpoint) 
 The list of ANR labels in the reverse direction (the path from the remote RTP endpoint to the node containing the PLU) 
 The maximum packet size, which is the value of the smallest link size along the route between the RTP endpoints. 
 The maximum amount of time that the remote RTP endpoint requires for a path switch. 
     The ROUTE_SETUP request is sent by the node containing the PLU and is processed by every node along the route, up to and including the remote RTP endpoint, to obtain the forward route information.  When the ROUTE_SETUP request reaches the remote RTP endpoint, a ROUTE_SETUP reply is sent back to gather the reverse route information. 
 
 Figure 1  shows an example of the flows during the ROUTE_SETUP process.   Figure 1. ROUTE_SETUP process         In the figure, a session between LUa (the PLU) in the  z/TPF system  and LUd in node D is starting.  The RSCV calculated by the network is a three-hop route, the  z/TPF system  determined that HPR support can be used for the entire route, and a new RTP connection will be started.  The step-by-step description of the ROUTE_SETUP process is as follows:     The  z/TPF system  receives a LOCATE command on the CP-CP sessions containing the RSCV. 
 The  z/TPF system  builds the ROUTE_SETUP request; the following information is included:     Req   The ROUTE_SETUP command is marked as a request. 
 PCIDx   A new procedure correlation identifier (PCID) to identify this ROUTE_SETUP process.  This is not the PCID of the LU-LU session being started. 
 RSCV   The route for the LU-LU session.
ROUTE_SETUP process
PCIDx   A new procedure correlation identifier (PCID) to identify this ROUTE_SETUP process.  This is not the PCID of the LU-LU session being started. 
 RSCV   The route for the LU-LU session. 
 DLU   Name of the destination LU, which, in this example, is LUd. 
 FANR   Forward ANR field. The  z/TPF system  includes the ANR label for the first link (which is A1) here. Each node along the route will add to this field. 
   
 Node B adds ANR label B2 to the FANR field and then, using the RSCV, passes the ROUTE_SETUP request to node C. 
 Node C adds ANR label C1 to the FANR field and then, using the RSCV, passes the ROUTE_SETUP request to node D. 
 Node D builds the ROUTE_SETUP reply; the following fields are included:     Rep   The ROUTE_SETUP command is a reply. 
 PCIDx   The PCID from the ROUTE_SETUP request. 
 CP_DLU   CP name of the remote RTP endpoint (CP name of node D). 
 FANR   Forward ANR field.  This is copied from the ROUTE_SETUP request. 
 NCE_DLU   NCE identifier assigned to the destination LU in the remote RTP endpoint, which is D4 in this example. 
 RANR   Reverse ANR field. The remote RTP endpoint puts ANR label D1 here. Each node along the route will add to this field. 
   
 Because the ROUTE_SETUP command is a reply, intermediate nodes add to the RANR field rather than the FANR field.  Node C adds ANR label C2 to the RANR field. 
 Node B adds ANR label B1 to the RANR field. 
     When the ROUTE_SETUP reply is received by the  z/TPF system , the RTP connection is started by sending out an NLP marked as a new connection. The NLP also contains the BIND request to start the new LU-LU session. 
 The ROUTE_SETUP process is also used during the path switch process. See  Path switches  for more information about the path switch process.
#

Answer: RPNオブジェクトでUTSを識別する方法は、RTP 接続が開始されたときに ROUTE_SETUP コマンドを使用して行います。このプロセスは、APPN 検索（LOCATE 流）の後、BIND 要求が送信される前に実行されます。ROUTE_SETUP プロセスの目的は、ルートに関する HPR 情報を収集することです。具体的には、以下の情報を取得します。   
- 前方方向（PLU が存在するノードからリモート RTP 端点へのパス）における ANR ラベルのリスト。   
- 後方方向（リモート RTP 端点から PLU が存在するノードへのパス）における ANR ラベルのリスト。   
- ルート上の最小リンクサイズに基づく最大パケットサイズ。   
- リモート RTP 端点がパス スイッチに必要とする最大時間。   
   
 ROUTE_SETUP 要求は、PLU が存在するノードから送信され、ルート上のすべてのノード（リモート RTP 端点を含む）で処理されます。この要求がリモート RTP 端点に到達すると、逆方向のルート情報を取得するために ROUTE_SETUP 応答が返されます。   
   
 このプロセスは、z/TPF システム と LUd の間のセッションが開始される例を示した図 1 で説明されています。z/TPF システム から LUd への RSCV が 3 ホップのルートで計算され、HPR サポートが全てのルートで使用可能であることが判明し、新しい RTP 接続が開始されます。STEP‑BY‑STEP での ROUTE_SETUP プロセスの説明は以下の通りです。   
   
 1. z/TPF システム が CP‑CP セッション内の RSCV を使用して LOCATE コマンドを受信します。   
 2. z/TPF システム が ROUTE_SETUP 要求を構築します。以下の情報が含まれます。   
    - Req   ROUTE_SETUP コマンドは要求としてマークされます。   
    - PCIDx   この ROUTE_SETUP プロセスを識別する新しい手順相関 ID (PCID)。これは、開始される LU‑LU セッションの PCID ではありません。   
    - RSCV   LU‑LU セッションのルート。   
    - DLU   宛先 LU の名前、この例では LUd。   
    - FANR   前方 ANR フィールド。z/TPF システム は最初のリンク（A1）の ANR ラベルをここに含めます。ルート上の各ノードはこのフィールドに ANR ラベルを追加します。   
   
 3. ノード B は FANR フィールドに ANR ラベル B2 を追加し、RSCV を使用してノード C に ROUTE_SETUP 要求を伝達します。   
 4. ノード C は FANR フィールドに ANR ラベル C1 を追加し、RSCV を使用してノード D に ROUTE_SETUP 要求を伝達します。   
 5. ノード D は ROUTE_SETUP 応答を構築します。以下のフィールドが含まれます。   
    - Rep   ROUTE_SETUP コマンドは応答です。   
    - PCIDx   ROUTE_SETUP 要求からの PCID。   
    - CP_DLU   リモート RTP 端点の CP 名（ノード D の CP 名）。   
    - FANR   前方 ANR フィールド。これは ROUTE_SETUP 要求からコピーされます。   
    - NCE_DLU   宛先 LU に割り当てられた NCE 識別子、この例では D4。   
    - RANR   後方 ANR フィールド。リモート RTP 端点はここに ANR ラベル D1 を入れます。ルート上の各ノードはこのフィールドに ANR ラベルを追加します。   
   
 6. ROUTE_SETUP コマンドが応答であるため、中間ノードは RANR フィールドに追加し、FANR フィールドではありません。ノード C は RANR フィールドに ANR ラベル C2 を追加します。ノード B は RANR フィールドに ANR ラベル B1 を追加します。   
   
 7. z/TPF システム が ROUTE_SETUP 応答を受信すると、RTP 接続は新しい接続の NLP を送信することで開始されます。NLP には、新しい LU‑LU セッションを開始するための BIND 要求も含まれています。   
   
 ROUTE_SETUP プロセスは、パス スイッチ プロセス中にも使用されます。パス スイッチ プロセスについては、別途「パス スイッチ」を参照してください。

Content: Db2 13 - Db2 SQL - BLOB scalar function
BLOB  scalar function   
 The BLOB function returns a BLOB representation of a string of any type or of a row ID type. 
   
 BLOB(  string-expression , integer ) 
       The schema is SYSIBM. 
   string-expression   An expression that returns a value that is a built-in character string, graphic string, binary string, or a row ID type. 
 integer   An integer value that specifies the length attribute of the resulting binary string.  The value must be an integer between 1 and the maximum length of a BLOB.   Do not specify  integer  if  string-expression  is a row ID type. 
 If you do not specify  integer  and  string-expression  is an empty string constant, the length attribute of the result is 1, and the result is an empty string. Otherwise, the length attribute of the result is the same as the length attribute of  string-expression , except when the input is graphic data. In this case, the length attribute of the result is twice the length of  expression . 
 
   The result of the function is a BLOB. 
 The result can be null; if the first argument is null, the result is the null value. 
 The actual length of the result is the minimum of the length attribute of the result and the actual length of  string-expression  (or twice the length of  string-expression  when the input is graphic data). If the length of  string-expression  is greater than the length attribute of the result, truncation is performed. A warning is returned unless the first input argument is a character string and all the truncated characters are blanks, or the first input argument is a graphic string and all the truncated characters are double-byte blanks. 
 
 Example 1:  The following function returns a BLOB for the string 'This is a BLOB'.      SELECT BLOB('This is a BLOB')
     FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1; 
   
 Example 2:  The following function returns a BLOB for the large object that is identified by locator myclob_locator.      SELECT BLOB(:myclob_locator)
     FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1;

     FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1; 
   
 Example 3:  Assume that a table has a BLOB column named TOPOGRAPHIC_MAP and a VARCHAR column named MAP_NAME. Locate any maps that contain the string 'Engles Island' and return a single binary string with the map name concatenated in front of the actual map.       SELECT BLOB(MAP_NAME || ':  ') || TOPOGRAPHIC_MAP
     FROM ONTARIO_SERIES_4
     WHERE TOPOGRAPHIC_MAP LIKE BLOB('%Engles Island%')

Content: Db2 13 - Db2 SQL - DBCLOB scalar function
DBCLOB  scalar function   
 The DBCLOB function returns a DBCLOB representation of a character string value (with the single-byte characters converted to double-byte characters) or a graphic string value. 
 

Character to DBCLOB:  
 
 DBCLOB(  character-expression , integer , CODEUNITS16 CODEUNITS32 )
Db2 13 - Db2 SQL - DBCLOB scalar function
Graphic to DBCLOB:  
 
 DBCLOB(  graphic-expression , integer , CODEUNITS16 CODEUNITS32 ) 
       The schema is SYSIBM. 
 Character to DBCLOB 
   character-expression   An expression that returns a value that is an EBCDIC-encoded or Unicode-encoded character string. It cannot be BIT data. The argument does not need to be mixed data, but any occurrences of  X'0E'  and  X'0F'  in the string must conform to the rules for EBCDIC mixed data. (See  Character strings  for these rules.) 
 integer   The length attribute of the resulting DBCLOB.  The value of  integer  must be between 1 and the maximum length of a DBCLOB, expressed in the units that are either implicitly or explicitly specified.   If CODEUNITS16 or CODEUNITS32 is specified, see  Determining the length attribute of the final result  for information about how to calculate the length attribute of the result string.  If CODEUNITS32 is specified, the value of  integer  must be between 1 and the maximum length of a DBCLOB divided by two (to allow for an intermediate result string that is long enough to evaluate the function). 
 If  integer  is not specified and  character-expression  is an empty string constant, the length attribute of the result is 1, and the result is an empty string. Otherwise, the length attribute of the result is the same as the length attribute of  character-expression . 
 
 CODEUNITS16  or  CODEUNITS32   Specifies the unit that is used to express  integer .  If CODEUNITS16 or CODEUNITS32 is specified, the input is EBCDIC, and there is no system CCSID for EBCDIC GRAPHIC data, an error occurs.    CODEUNITS16   Specifies that  integer  is expressed in terms of 16-bit UTF-16 code units. 
 CODEUNITS32   Specifies that  integer  is expressed in terms of 32-bit UTF-32 code units. 
   For more information about CODEUNITS16 and CODEUNITS32, see  String unit specifications .

Content: Common tasks for using  REST 
   You can refer to one or more of these common tasks to explore  REST  on the  z/TPF system . 
     
 Deploying z/TPF traditional services to be consumed by remote clients  For a  REST  service call from a remote client that requests a  z/TPF  traditional service, you must deploy the service to the  z/TPF system . 
 
 Deploying z/TPF Java services to be consumed by remote clients  For a  REST  service call from a remote client that requests a  z/TPF  Java™ service, you must deploy the service to the  z/TPF system . 
 
 Calling local or remote services from z/TPF applications  You can call  REST  services that are provided by the  z/TPF system  or a remote system. 
 
 Calling local Java services from z/TPF applications  You can create an application service in Java™ that can be called by  z/TPF  assembler and C/C++ applications by using the  tpf_srvcInvoke  function. 
 
 Generating a REST service call with an OpenAPI descriptor  With the  z/TPF OpenAPI code generation utility (tpfrestgen) , you can use an  OpenAPI descriptor  as the starting point to generate a REST service call that can be integrated into an existing  z/TPF  application.
#

Content: REST   
 Representational State Transfer (REST)  is a stateless architecture that can be used to provide interoperability between heterogeneous computer systems. 
   REST  services are often implemented by using  Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)  with data sent in the format of   JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) .  OpenAPI specification , which is also know as Swagger, is one of the most popular standards for describing  REST  services.  
       
 REST provider support   REST provider support  uses the  z/TPF HTTP server  to implement a  REST  service provider by creating an  OpenAPI descriptor  to describe the  REST  service and a  z/TPF service descriptor  to describe the  z/TPF  implementation details for that service. 
 
 REST consumer support  With  REST consumer support , a  z/TPF  application can call a  REST  service on a remote system through the  z/TPF   HTTP client  or call a service on the  z/TPF system . 
 
 REST message handlers   REST message handlers  provide additional processing that can be specified at a REST services level and shared among multiple REST services. 
 
 Common tasks for using REST  You can refer to one or more of these common tasks to explore  REST  on the  z/TPF system . 
 
 z/TPF scriptable code coverage support   z/TPF scriptable code coverage support  provides  REST  services for you to collect code coverage data for your  z/TPF  applications. 
 
 z/TPF OpenAPI code generation utility (tpfrestgen)  The  z/TPF OpenAPI code generation utility (tpfrestgen)  helps you to create  REST service  consumers or  REST service  providers that are described by an  OpenAPI descriptor . 
 
 REST API reference  The  z/TPF system  supports various  REST  APIs that client applications can use to access  z/TPF  resources. 
 
 Supported OpenAPI Specification version 2.0  The  z/TPF system  supports a subset of the  OpenAPI  Specification version 2.0.
#

Content: REST consumer support   
 With  REST consumer support , a  z/TPF  application can call a  REST  service on a remote system through the  z/TPF   HTTP client  or call a service on the  z/TPF system . 
 The  z/TPF system  builds the request data structure that is sent by a  z/TPF  application into an HTTP request, transforms the HTTP response into a response data structure, and passes back the response to the calling application. The  z/TPF   HTTP client  is used to make the service call to the remote system that contains the  REST  service. 
 REST consumer support  also supports persistent connections for  REST  services by using the  high-speed connector . 
       
 REST consumer message flow  The  z/TPF system  builds a  REST  service request that is sent by a  z/TPF  application, transforms the response into a single response structure and passes back the response to the application.
#

 Method   The HTTP method that is applied to the URL. 
 Description   The description about what the API is used for. 
 API documentation   The implementation details about the API. Most  REST  APIs are provided with an  OpenAPI descriptor  that describes the implementation details of the API. You can use the  Swagger Editor  to view an  OpenAPI descriptor . If an  OpenAPI descriptor  is not provided, see the referenced topic for the details about the API. 
  The APIs are grouped by the resources on the  z/TPF system . The following resources are available for client applications to call in  REST :   REST APIs for service management 
 REST provider services

Developing REST artifacts
About this task    You can use  TPF Toolkit  to develop the following types of  REST  artifacts: 
 
 
 Table 1. REST artifacts 
 
 
 
 
 
     File type   File extension   Description   
       OpenAPI descriptor       .swagger.json 
 .openapi.json

   z/TPF service descriptor   .srvc.json   Describes the implementation information for a  z/TPF service .

 Adding parameters to the OpenAPI descriptor  Use the context menu to add parameter objects to the  OpenAPI descriptor . 
 
 Adding responses to the OpenAPI descriptor  Use the context menu to add response objects to the  OpenAPI descriptor . 
 
 Adding definitions to the OpenAPI descriptor  Use the context menu to add definition objects to the  OpenAPI descriptor .

Content: LOADVFCB
IMAGE  imagelib 
   specifies the image library that contains the specified FCB. If you do not specify the IMAGE option, you get the default image library for the device type. The default image library is IMAG xxxx , where  xxxx  is the device type; for example, the default image library is IMAG1403 for a 1403 type printer.
LOADVFCB
Usage Notes      The virtual FCB image should match the FCB image on the real printer. If it does not, results are unpredictable.  If the spool file is printed on a real 1403 printer, the virtual FCB image is ignored, and channel skipping is controlled by the carriage tape. 
 
 If you are running a program in your virtual machine that requires printer overflow sensing information and you are printing on a real 1403, you need to take special steps to retrieve the sensing information. First, ensure that the CP directory entry for your virtual machine indicates that the printer is a 3203, 3211, 3262, 4245, or 4248, even though the program and the guest operating system in which the program runs define the printer as a 1403. Then use the LOADVFCB command to specify a virtual FCB image that matches the 1403. CP uses this virtual FCB image as a basis for retrieving sensing information. 
 If the virtual machine operating system issues a LOAD FCB channel command word to the virtual spooled printer, the LOAD FCB CCW image replaces the virtual FCB image provided on the LOADVFCB command line. Note that the CMS PRINT command issues a LOAD FCB CCW and thereby replaces the virtual FCB image. 
 The LOADVFCB command allows specification of the extended FCB image for a virtual 4248 printer. If an attempt is made to send the extended FCB image to a printer that does not support the extended FCB format, an error message results. 
 If the default FCB image has been modified, the virtual FCB image from the spooled printer is stored in any file created on that printer. When the file is printed on a real printer, the FCB is loaded into the real printer according to the FILEFCB or DEFFCB option specified on the START command. The file then prints properly on the real printer.

Content: Remote-to-local file mapping   
 When you define a remote system, you  map  (associate) the lowest level qualifier in each MVS data set name to a file name extension for the related workstation file.   IBM® Explorer for z/OS®  includes a set of defined remote-to-local file mappings. The **COBOL file mapping, for example, maps MVS files with a low-level qualifier  COBOL  to workstation files with the  .cbl  file name extension. 1     

Mapping  
 A mapping indicates how  IBM Explorer for z/OS  processes file transfers between z/OS and the workstation; specifically, the mapping indicates whether file transfers are based on an exchange of text (in which case ASCII/EBCDIC conversions occur) or on an exchange of binary data. A mapping also helps you to know, at a glance, the general purpose of a particular file. 
 If you use the same low-level qualifier for several data sets, the same mappings affect file transfers for each of those data sets. Given the mappings that are included in  IBM Explorer for z/OS , for example, you can transfer members of the partitioned data sets  USER01.COBOL  and  USER01.TEST.COBOL  to and from workstation-based files that have the extension  .cbl . 2 
 You can see remote-to-local file mappings in the  z/OS File System Mapping  view of the  RSE perspective  perspective. The following screen capture shows this view. 
  You can customize these mappings to match the naming conventions on your remote system either through the  z/OS File System Mapping  view or on the  Mapping  page of the  Properties  window. For more information about customizing these mappings, see  Mapping data sets and partitioned data set members . For more information about the properties of file mappings, see the remaining sections of this topic.
Remote-to-local file mapping
Workstation file extension  
 The type of a file is indicated by its workstation file extension. In the mappings that are shown in the screen capture, a  .cbl  extension, for example, is considered to be a COBOL source file. Each file can have only one file type. JCL with embedded COBOL source, for example, is not supported. The default workstation file extension for a new mapping is undefined. 
   

Transfer mode  
 The transfer mode can be either text, indicating that a conversion between ASCII and EBCDIC occurs, or binary. The default transfer mode for a new mapping is text. 
   

Code page  
 Each file can have only one code page, but you can specify a group of files as having the same code page. When you specify code pages, specify both a local and a host code page and keep them consistent. The default host and local code pages for a new mapping are inherited from the system properties of the remote and local file systems. 
 For a list of supported host code pages, see  Supported host code pages . The availability of local code pages is based on the text file encodings that are supported by the Eclipse text editor. Be sure to specify code pages to be consistent with the compiler settings of your files.

[Rank 1] Title: IBM z/Transaction Processing Facility Enterprise Edition DB0111
URL: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/ztpf/1.1.2025?topic=db0000db9999-db0111
Score: 0.12440895289182663
Content: DB0111       

Last updated    Changed for  PUT02 . 
   

Program    Displayed on the console and in the dump. 
   

Error message    fileid  PFA  pfaddr   rcc  CFA  cfaddr 
   

Where      fileid   The file identifier (ID). 
 pfaddr   The prime file address. 
 rcc   The record code check. 
 cfaddr   The current file address. 
     

Explanation  
 A  z/TPFDF  macro or function was issued that requires a tape name, but one of the following errors occurred:     The application program did not specify a tape name. 
 An incorrect tape name was specified. 
 A valid tape name was specified, but the tape is not mounted. 
     This error can occur when using the following:     
 DBTRD  macro 
 
 DBTLG  macro 
 
 DBOPN  macro with the TAPE parameter 
 
 dftrd  function 
 
 dftlg  function 
 
 dfopn  function with the tape name parameter. 
       

System action  
 If the application has specified that return-optional  z/TPFDF  system errors should return control, control returns to the application program with bit 0 of SW00RTN and bit 7 of SW00RT2 set to 1.  Otherwise, the  entry control block  ( ECB ) exits. 
   

User response  
 
 Complete the following steps:   Ensure the application program is specifying a valid tape name. 
 Verify that the tape is properly mounted before running the application program. 
       

Related information    For more information about how return-optional  z/TPFDF  system errors should return control, the  DBTRD ,  DBTLG , and  DBOPN  macros, and the  dftrd ,  dftlg , and  dfopn  functions, see  z/TPFDF Programming Concepts and Reference .
#

Table 6. Information of each bundled product
This API retrieves the following information per each bundled product:
This API retrieves the following information per each bundled product: Table 6. Information of each bundled product API: productName, Description: The name of the detected bundled product. API: productId, Description: The identifier of the bundled product. API: metricName, Description: The list of metrics of the parent IBM Cloud Paks or IBM Solution Bundle. API: metricPeakDate, Description: The date when the license usage of the bundled product was the highest within the requested period. API: metricMeasuredQuantity, Description: The highest number of license units that the bundled product used within the requested period. API: cloudpakId, Description: The identification number of the IBM Cloud Pak® to which the program is bundled. API: cloudpakVersion, Description: Version of the IBM Cloud Pak® to which the program is bundled. API: cloudpakMetricName, Description: The license metric unit that is used by the entire IBM Cloud Pak® to which the bundled product contributes. API: metricConversion, Description: The ratio that shows how the license usage of the bundled product is counted when compared with the license usage of the IBM Cloud Pak®. It shows how the program's license metrics are recalculated when compared to the IBM Cloud Pak®  license metrics. API: metricConvertedQuantity, Description: The number of license units that the bundled product contributed to the overall license usage of the IBM Cloud Pak®. The value is calculated by comparing metricMeasuredQuantity against metricConversion.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB   
 
 With  z/TPF support for MongoDB , remote distributed platforms can access and update data in a  z/TPF  database by using the  MongoDB Query Language .   You do not need to change  z/TPF  application code to use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .   MongoDB  is a NoSQL database and treats data as documents.  MongoDB  documents are described by using   JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) , which is an open and human- and machine-readable standard to facilitate data exchange. The  z/TPF  database is not a NoSQL database, but you can create a  JSON  document from the data in the  z/TPF  database. 
       
 Access z/TPF data by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  The  z/TPF   Internet Daemon  ( InetD ) is used to access the  z/TPF  data by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  z/TPF support for MongoDB  is provided only for  z/TPFDF  databases.  
 
 MongoDB terminology  Some concepts in  z/TPFDF  and  MongoDB  are similar, but the terms to refer to these concepts might be different. 
 
 z/TPFDF database definition (DBDEF) considerations   z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports only R-type  z/TPFDF  files. Some settings in the  z/TPFDF  database definitions change the behavior of  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Add default keys by using z/TPFDF default key support  With  z/TPFDF default key support for z/TPF support for MongoDB , you can define default keys for  z/TPFDF  files in the  z/TPFDF collection descriptors  ( adbi.xml  files). 
 
 Setting up z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must define a  z/TPF  server for  MongoDB  before you can connect  MongoDB  remote clients to the  z/TPF system  by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .
z/TPF support for MongoDB
Preparing the z/TPF system for data access by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You must prepare the  z/TPF system  before you can access  z/TPF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB . 
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB security  To maintain a secure environment, you must implement controls to ensure that users have access only to data that they are authorized to access.  
 
 z/TPF user security   By using  z/TPF user security , you can define  z/TPF  user IDs, passwords, and privileges to  z/TPF  data and resources. You can use  z/TPF user security  only for   z/TPF support for MongoDB  applications.  
 
 Analyze the performance of z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can use   resource usage by owner name collection  on the  z/TPF system  to collect resource usage information for the  MongoDB  applications based on the owner name. You can specify the high-level qualifier and mid-level qualifier in the  resource usage by owner name configuration file  to collect resource usage information by specific categories.  
 
 Operations and coverage considerations for z/TPF support for MongoDB  There are operational considerations to remember when you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 User exits for MongoDB request processing  For each  MongoDB  request,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  provides two user exits, the pre-request user exit (UMON_pre_request) and post-request user exit (UMON_post_request) for you to control pre-request and post-request processing.  
 
 Filter collections by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  A filtered collection is a logical subset or view of a collection or a subset of logical records (LRECs) of a  z/TPFDF  file. As a database administrator, you can use filtered collections to control the visibility of the data in a collection.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB  ( APARs  PJ42292 and PI33010)   
 z/TPF support for MongoDB   provides the ability to access  z/TPFDF  databases from remote distributed systems by using the standard  MongoDB  query language without requiring changes to z/TPF applications.  
 Previously, to request access to the  z/TPF  data on the  z/TPF system  from a remote distributed system, custom applications were required on the  z/TPF system  and the remote distributed systems that access the  z/TPF  data. The custom  z/TPF  applications required accessing the  z/TPF  databases and formatting  z/TPF  binary data for the remote distributed system applications. Implementing the custom applications on the  z/TPF system  might have the following results:   The implementation of the custom interfaces was time consuming.  
 
 z/TPF  application programmers and remote application developers were involved to maintain custom interfaces.  
 Different custom interfaces might need to be developed and deployed, because remote distributed systems might require different formats and functionality.  
     With  z/TPF support for MongoDB , remote distributed systems can access the  z/TPFDF  databases by using the standard  MongoDB  clients. Standard  MongoDB  clients exist in different programming languages, and you can install standard  MongoDB  clients on different remote distributed platforms.  
 z/TPF support for MongoDB  supports many  MongoDB  programming services. With these  MongoDB  programming services, you can get information or access documents in the  z/TPFDF  databases.  
 Accessing  z/TPFDF  databases by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB  does not require any changes to the  z/TPF  applications. However, to use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , the code must be built with the  GCC  4.6 ( version tpf-11r1-13 or later ) or the Dignus Systems/C or Systems/C++ V1.98 (version 1.98.68 or later) compiler.  
 For more information about  APARs   PJ42292  and PI33010, see the APEDITs.

Content: z/TPF support for MongoDB  programming   
 This information describes the  MongoDB  programming methodology that is used to interface with  z/TPF  data. 
 Examples that are provided in this information are one of the following types:   Programmatic examples that use the  MongoDB  Java™ client driver . 
 Shell based examples that describe the actual input document. You can use standard shell-based tools to send requests from a graphical user interface (GUI) or command line.  
           
 Connect to z/TPF support for MongoDB on the z/TPF system   
 
 Access the z/TPF database by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  When the  MongoDB  remote client connects to the  z/TPF system  and the  MongoDB  remote client is authenticated, the  MongoDB  remote client can access the  z/TPF  database.  
 
 Retrieve collections by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can retrieve individual collections from the  z/TPF  database after  MongoDB  remote clients access the database, for example, a  z/TPFDF  file that is named PNR.  
 
 Understand the ObjectId value in z/TPF support for MongoDB  In standard  MongoDB , documents that are saved in a collection require a unique ID field to be associated with the document. The ObjectId value is the representation of this unique identifier. In the  z/TPF system , the ObjectId value represents the file address of the prime block of the  z/TPFDF  subfile, which is unique for every subfile in a  z/TPFDF  file. The ObjectId value, in the  z/TPF system , is a 12-byte value that consists of an 8-byte hexadecimal file address that is right justified. 
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB data definition considerations  When you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , the  DFDL schema file  describes the contents of the  z/TPFDF  file. The  DFDL schema file  for the  z/TPFDF  file defines the field names and data types for the  z/TPFDF  binary data.
z/TPF support for MongoDB programming
Use automatic indexing rules for z/TPF support for MongoDB  With standard  MongoDB  servers, you can add indexes for fields in the document that allows optimized retrieval when the document is located by using that field. The indexes for these fields are maintained by the standard  MongoDB  server. Maintenance of these indexes is transparent to the end user who accesses the standard  MongoDB  server. 
 
 Retrieve documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can retrieve the documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you get a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Insert documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can insert documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Update documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can update documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Remove documents by using z/TPF support for MongoDB  You can remove documents, or  z/TPFDF  subfiles, after you obtain a collection by using  z/TPF support for MongoDB .  
 
 Logging for z/TPF support for MongoDB  With logging for  z/TPF support for MongoDB , you can log  MongoDB  requests and responses and send the logging data to a server in binary JSON (BSON) format.  
 
 z/TPF support for MongoDB error messages  When you use  z/TPF support for MongoDB , certain situations might   cause the  z/TPF   MongoDB  server to return  an error. For example,  z/TPF support for MongoDB  returns an error to the  MongoDB  client when a user tries to update a document but does not have authority to update.

 There are four types of objects in the Git object model: 
   blob 				   is used to store file data

 ObjectId head = repository.resolve("HEAD");    Ref   A ref is a variable that holds a single object identifier. The object identifier can be any valid Git object (blob, tree, commit, tag).

These are the default decorations: 
     
     dirty (folder)  - At least one file below the folder is dirty; that means that it has changes in the working tree that are neither in the index nor in the repository. 			 
   tracked  - The resource is known to the Git repository and hence under version control. 			 
   untracked  - The resource is not known to the Git repository and will not be version controlled until it is explicitly added. 			 
   ignored  - The resource is ignored by the Git team provider. The preference settings under  				 Team > Ignored Resources , "derived" flag and settings from  .gitignore  files are taken into account. 			 
   dirty  - The resource has changes in the working tree that are neither in the index nor in the repository. 			 
   staged  - The resource has changes which have been added to the index. Note that adding changes to the index is currently possible only in the commit dialog via the context menu of a resource. 			 
   partially-staged  - The resource has changes which are added to the index and additional changes in the working tree that neither reached the index nor have been committed to the repository. See  				 partial staging from the Git Staging view  for how to do that. 			 
   added  - The resource has not yet reached any commit in the repository but has been freshly added to the Git repository in order to be tracked in future. 			 
   removed  - The resource is staged for removal from the Git repository. 			 
   conflict  - A merge conflict exists for the file. 			 
   assume-valid  - The resource has the "assume unchanged" flag. This means that Git stops checking the working tree files for possible modifications, so you need to manually unset the bit to tell Git when you change the working tree file. Also see  				 Assume unchanged action .
